documents: Laissez-passer for a corpse (salconduit mortuori) from the competent authority of the departure state, for coffins from Strasbourg Agreement countries

From other countries: the Spanish consulate's Documento Unico (or the French equivalent) for the arrival airport, issued on the death certificate, medical certificate of cause of death, embalming or temporary-conservation certificate and judicial permit if the death was violent
Entry authorisation from Spanish Sanidad Exterior (requested by the funeral company through SISAEX) when the coffin lands in Spain
Death certificate from the country of death
AD.coffin: Strasbourg Agreement standard (Art. 6, reproduced in Andorra's official gazette): watertight coffin with absorbent material, either an outer wooden coffin (sides at least 20 mm) with an inner soldered zinc coffin, or a single wooden coffin (at least 30 mm) lined with zinc; for air transport, a purifying (pressure-equalising) device or guarantees of strength accepted by the departure authority. No separate Andorran entry standard is published.
AD.embalming: No Andorran entry rule is published; the departure country's rules apply. Spain, the usual arrival point, requires an embalming or temporary-conservation certificate in its consular procedure for coffins from countries outside the Strasbourg and Berlin agreements.
AD.consular: No Andorran consular permit is needed from Strasbourg states: the departure state's laissez-passer suffices and transit or destination states cannot refuse it. Andorra's competent authority for issuing laissez-passers is the Servei de Medicina Forense (Departament de Medicina Legal, attached to the ministry of justice and interior). From other countries, the coffin needs the Spanish consulate's Documento Unico for entry at a Spanish airport (or the French procedure if landing in France).
AD.arrival: Customs and health clearance take place at the Spanish or French arrival airport (in Spain, the funeral company requests the Sanidad Exterior entry authorisation through SISAEX, then customs releases the coffin). An Andorran funeral director drives the coffin into Andorra. Confirm burial or cremation formalities with the Andorran funeral director.
AD.private_aviation: Andorra has no airport usable by business jets. Plan the flight into Barcelona, Girona, Toulouse or another Spanish or French airport with customs and health services, and a road transfer by an Andorran funeral director. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket.
AD.export: An Andorran funeral home prepares the body and seals the coffin. For Strasbourg states, the Servei de Medicina Forense issues the laissez-passer for a corpse once Andorran medical, health, administrative and legal formalities are met and the coffin meets the Agreement's conditions. Other destinations may require their consulate's approval. Shipments usually leave by road to a Spanish or French airport, where their transit rules apply. Confirm delays with the funeral director.
AD.authority: Servei de Medicina Forense (Departament de Medicina Legal, ministry of justice and interior); Spanish Sanidad Exterior at the arrival airport

documents: Death certificate attested by the country of death and by the UAE embassy, with certified Arabic translation (official u.ae list for UAE nationals)
Report on the cause of death (UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs, for UAE nationals)
Embalming certificate and certificate of sealed casket (expected; confirm with the consulate)
Copy of the deceased's passport and airway bill
AE.coffin: No official UAE import standard for the casket was found. Use a hermetically sealed, zinc-lined casket in an outer wooden case meeting IATA/airline requirements; confirm with the UAE consulate.
AE.embalming: Embalming is required for remains leaving the UAE (gov.uk). For incoming remains, embalming is expected but not confirmed by an official UAE source.
AE.consular: For UAE nationals who die abroad, the UAE embassy in the country of death attests the death certificate and translates it into Arabic. For non-UAE nationals being buried in the UAE, confirm requirements with the UAE consulate.
AE.arrival: No official arrival procedure was found. The receiving funeral service collects the casket after customs and health clearance; confirm the timing with it. A burial in the UAE needs a burial permit from the district police (u.ae).
AE.private_aviation: No official rule specific to private or charter flights carrying human remains was found for the UAE. Remains are cleared like air cargo: plan arrival at an international airport with customs and health staff, and have the handling agent and the receiving funeral home confirm clearance before departure.
AE.export: The death must be registered and an official death certificate issued; MOFA stamps and signs the certificate and its translation. The deceased's embassy issues a no-objection letter and cancels the passport; the residency visa is cancelled. Police issue a no-objection letter, with copies for the airport police, embalming facility and mortuary. The body must be embalmed and the coffin must meet specific rules; 7 photocopies of each document travel with the body. Non-Muslims may be cremated instead. Deaths outside hospital go to the police and the body is released only with the prosecutor's permission. Confirm delays with the funeral director.
AE.authority: UAE embassy/consulate abroad; Ministry of Foreign Affairs; police and Ministry of Health and Prevention (exit)

documents: Death certificate with apostille (or legalisation) from the country of death
Passport or ID card of the deceased
Body transport permit (laissez-passer) issued by the Albanian consulate
Funeral director's documents from the country of death (e.g. embalming and sealing certificates, local removal permit; confirm with the consulate)
AL.coffin: A special transport casket is required. Albanian official pages do not publish the technical specification; international practice (sealed metal-lined inner coffin in a wooden outer case) is expected. Confirm with the Albanian consulate.
AL.embalming: No published Albanian rule on embalming for incoming remains was found; it is normally done in the country of departure. Confirm with the Albanian consulate and the funeral director.
AL.consular: The Albanian consulate issues the body transport permit (laissez-passer) once the apostilled death certificate and the deceased's passport or ID are submitted in person by the family or the funeral company. The London consulate states the permit is issued immediately once documents are complete. The consulate does not issue apostilles.
AL.arrival: The casket is cleared at the airport and collected by an Albanian funeral home. Ask the funeral home about registering the death with the local civil status office. No burial deadline published for repatriated remains.
AL.private_aviation: No specific rules published for private flights carrying remains. Use an airport with customs and border control (Tirana International). Carry the consular laissez-passer and apostilled death certificate on board.
AL.export: Leaving Albania: a local funeral director shows the death certificate, obtains permission to remove the body and provides a special transport casket; the deceased's passport is required. Albanian death certificates do not state the cause of death; an international version with English translation can be requested. Cremation is not available in Albania (it can be arranged in a neighbouring country). The destination country's consulate rules also apply.
AL.authority: Albanian embassy or consulate (Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs); local Civil Status Office

documents: Full death certificate, legalised by the foreign ministry of the country of death (Lisbon consulate: issued within the last 6 months)
Transport/transfer permit issued by the local authority of the country of death (in Portugal: PSP 'alvara de trasladacao'), legalised
Medical health certificate (atestado medico sanitario), legalised
Deceased's passport or Angolan ID (may be asked; confirm with the consulate)
Portuguese translations by an official translator for documents in another language (London consulate practice for death records)
AO.coffin: Not published by Angolan authorities. A hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin in an outer wooden case is the international standard and should be expected; confirm with the consulate.
AO.embalming: Not specified in official Angolan sources found; embalming is normally performed for long-haul transfer. Confirm with the consulate.
AO.consular: The Angolan Consulate General handles the transfer (trasladacao) request. Lisbon requires the full death certificate (issued within 6 months), the PSP transfer permit and the medical health certificate, each legalised by the Portuguese foreign ministry, originals with one photocopy each; it states 8 working days, no fee, and may ask for extra documents or an interview. For death-record transcription, the London consulate requires official Portuguese translation, notarisation, FCDO authentication and consular authentication; confirm whether the same applies to a transfer file.
AO.arrival: Customs and health clearance at Luanda airport; a funeral agent collects the casket. No official arrival procedure or burial deadline was found; confirm with the receiving funeral agent.
AO.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A casket on a private aircraft should arrive at an international airport with customs and health (port health) officers, with landing permission arranged through a local handling agent, and the original documents travelling with the casket.
AO.export: The next of kin instructs a funeral agent (signed authority to proceed), who registers the death with the Angolan Civil Registration Office (mandatory, can take some time) and handles local procedures. Sudden, accidental or suspicious deaths involve the police and Public Prosecutor; post-mortem reports may take months. Angolan law sets no timescale for repatriation. Storage facilities in morgues vary by region.
AO.authority: Consulates of the Republic of Angola (Ministry of External Relations, MIREX)

documents: Death certificate (Argentine consulates in Australia ask for two copies), with Hague apostille
Certificate from the local health authority that the deceased did not die of a contagious disease, apostilled
Funeral home certificate of embalming and placement in a sealed, waterproof approved container or air tray, notarised where required and apostilled
Entry request filed by the funeral home with Argentine authorities stating date, place of shipment and destination
Some consulates (e.g. London) also ask for a local removal ('out of country') certificate and Spanish translations
AR.coffin: Argentine consulates require the body to be prepared under international transport rules and placed in a sealed, waterproof coffin (or approved container / air tray), certified by the funeral home. No official specification of zinc lining or of an official witness to the sealing was found; in practice a metal-lined sealed coffin is used.
AR.embalming: Expected: the Argentine consulate in New York requires a funeral home certificate (embalming report) confirming embalming; other consulates (Sydney, London) ask for a funeral home certificate on preparation of the remains under international transport rules. Confirm with the consulate and airline.
AR.consular: All documents need a Hague apostille from the country of death (consular legalisation only for non-Hague countries); some consulates also require a Spanish translation. Argentine consulates state they do not legalise these documents and do not grant permits to repatriate remains: documents go directly to the airline. Argentina is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Registering the death at the consulate is advisable for civil records.
AR.arrival: The Argentine funeral home receives the coffin and handles customs and health clearance and the burial or cremation under provincial or municipal rules. The national border health service (Direccion de Sanidad de Fronteras) is the competent health authority at ports of entry; current non-COVID filing rules are not published online, so confirm with the receiving funeral home.
AR.private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights was found. The aircraft must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services. Because the consulate process relies on the airline receiving the documents, on a charter the operator and the ground handler take that role: give them the apostilled originals and make sure the funeral home's entry request names the private flight and arrival airport.
AR.export: An Argentine funeral home obtains the civil registry death certificate (usually within 1 to 3 days), the embalming certificate and the certificate permitting transfer of the remains abroad, and supplies the special international casket. The destination country decides whether Argentine documents need an apostille. If a judge is involved (autopsy, violent or unexplained death) the judge must release the body and may delay it until test results are in; UK guidance says local formalities usually take 2 to 4 weeks.
AR.authority: Direccion de Sanidad de Fronteras (Ministry of Health) at the border; Argentine funeral home files the entry request

documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death, with English translation if needed (required unless embalmed)
Consular mortuary certificate and transit permit from the US embassy or consulate when there is no death certificate (for US citizens)
Embalming certificate if embalmed
CDC import permit only if the death involved an infectious agent and the body is not embalmed
Any American Samoa local clearance (not published; confirm with the funeral home)
AS.coffin: Federal rule: remains must be fully contained in a leak-proof container (double-layered puncture-resistant body bag, casket with certified leak-proof lining, or sealed metal transfer case). Hermetic sealing is not a federal requirement; airlines may require it.
AS.embalming: Not required by federal rules. Embalmed remains need no CDC permit; unembalmed remains need a death certificate or importer certification.
AS.consular: For US citizens who die abroad, the US embassy or consulate issues the consular report of death and mortuary documents. Remains from independent Samoa come under that country's own export rules.
AS.arrival: Remains not embalmed and without a CDC permit must be consigned directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory. Customs and any local health formalities in Pago Pago are not published online: confirm with the receiving funeral home. Death records: Office of Vital Statistics (American Samoa Department of Homeland Security), Pago Pago.
AS.pouch: Federal rules accept a double-layered, puncture-resistant, leak-proof body bag; airline and local acceptance must be confirmed.
AS.private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights carrying remains was found. Plan arrival at Pago Pago International Airport with customs available, and make sure the remains meet the federal CDC rules on arrival.
AS.export: Local export procedure not published online. The death is recorded by the Office of Vital Statistics; confirm any health clearance, embalming and casket requirements with the local funeral home and the destination country's consulate.
AS.authority: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (import, 42 CFR 71.55); American Samoa Office of Vital Statistics (death records)

documents: Leichenpass (laissez-passer for a corpse) from the authority of the place of death or an Austrian mission abroad
Death certificate
Embalming certificate where required by the departure country
AT.coffin: Austria applies the 1937 Berlin agreement (BGBl. 118/1958) and the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement (BGBl. 515/1978): a hermetically sealed coffin, normally a soldered zinc inner coffin in a wooden outer coffin with absorbent material. If no Leichenpass is presented, customs inspect the coffin or shipping case for serious damage, opening marks, leaks or strong odour.
AT.embalming: Embalming is not standard in Austria and no Austrian rule requiring it for incoming bodies was found; it is usually done only when the destination (or departure) country requires it.
AT.consular: An Austrian embassy or consulate can issue the Leichenpass and helps organise the transfer to Austria, which must be handled by a local funeral company working with an Austrian one. Costs are borne by the family or insurer.
AT.arrival: Customs clear the coffin when a Leichenpass is presented. Without one, customs release it only if the coffin is intact; if it is damaged or leaking, the municipal doctor decides on release in writing. Only licensed funeral companies may transport the body inside Austria; burial rules are set by each federal state.
AT.private_aviation: Austrian customs apply the Leichenpass check to every body brought into Austria, not only to imports from outside the EU, so a private flight from another EU state still needs customs clearance of the coffin at the arrival airport. Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
AT.export: The district administrative authority of the place of death (Bezirkshauptmannschaft or city Magistrat; the mayor in Lower Austria) issues the multilingual Leichenpass on application by the family or the funeral company, once the post-mortem inspection (Totenbeschau) is done, the death is registered and burial is released. Only licensed funeral companies may transport the body. Each federal state sets its own procedure and fees (e.g. Tyrol). The destination country may require further documents.

documents: Copy of the official death certificate (or register extract) stating the cause of death
If no cause of death is available: a medical practitioner's statement that the body shows no sign of communicable disease
Without these documents: permission from a Commonwealth Human Biosecurity Officer
Embalming certificate and export or transit permit required by the country of death and the airline
AU.coffin: The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing's human remains guidance requires remains for burial or cremation to arrive in a hermetically sealed container and to be moved from the port of arrival under the direction or control of a coroner or funeral director. In practice a sealed, usually zinc-lined, coffin in an outer case meeting IATA/airline rules is used.
AU.embalming: Not set as an Australian import requirement in the pages consulted; embalming is normally required by the country of departure and by airlines. NSW Health notes that embalming is generally required for international transport, with freezing or dry ice as an alternative.
AU.consular: No Australian consular legalisation requirement for incoming remains was found in official guidance; the departure country's export rules and documents apply. English translations are advisable; confirm with the Australian funeral director.
AU.arrival: Remains are subject to human biosecurity controls on arrival and move under the control of a funeral director or coroner. No import declaration is required for remains brought in for burial or cremation; the department prefers at least 48 hours' (weekday) notice before arrival. Burial or cremation then follows state or territory rules.
AU.private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights carrying human remains was found. Arrive at an international airport with border and biosecurity clearance, present the casket and its documents for human biosecurity clearance, and have a funeral director meet the aircraft.
AU.export: To send a body abroad, the funeral director gathers the death certificate, medical certificate of cause of death, embalming certificate and, where the destination requires it, a transit or no-objection letter from the state health authority (for example NSW Public Health Units need documents at least 48 hours ahead; Victoria's Department of Health issues repatriation letters, also with 48 hours notice). Embalming is generally required, with freezing or dry ice as an alternative if the receiving country accepts it. The destination consulate may add requirements.
AU.authority: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing (human biosecurity) with the Australian Border Force

documents: Medical statement from the competent doctor where the death occurred, or an extract of the death certificate (name, birth date/age, date and place of death, cause of death or statement that death was natural / not due to a contagious disease)
Statement from the person who embalmed or otherwise preserved the body, describing the method used
Statement from the competent authority of the place of death on how and by which route the body will be transported (transfer permit)
Strasbourg 1973 laissez-passer when coming from a Strasbourg Agreement state (explicitly recognised in the cremation rules)
AW.coffin: Hermetically sealed coffin made of impermeable material with absorbent material, containing only the body, its clothing, packing material and personal effects, packed to the satisfaction of the doctor designated by the Minister of Public Works and Public Health in a well-closing outer coffin. Name, first names, date of birth, date and place of death and destination must be clearly marked on the coffin. The law does not say who must witness the sealing at origin.
AW.embalming: Required: the body must be embalmed or properly preserved by another method. If the death was due to a quarantinable disease, arterial and cavity embalming is mandatory.
AW.consular: No specific consular step is set by the law; the transport statement must come from the competent authority of the country of death. Confirm legalisation (apostille) and translation needs with the receiving funeral home.
AW.arrival: Documents are presented on arrival; customs and the health authority clear the coffin. Bodies brought into Aruba must be buried as soon as possible and only with free written leave from the civil registrar (ambtenaar van de burgerlijke stand), which cannot be issued before the death statement is produced. For cremation, the customs officer must receive the Strasbourg laissez-passer (if from a party state) or an equivalent statement from the origin authority, and cremation takes place as soon as possible after 5 working days.
AW.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private aircraft. A private flight must land at the international airport with customs and health clearance; the same coffin and document rules apply as for cargo. Arrange collection by a local funeral home at the airport.
AW.export: Leaving Aruba: the same rules apply in reverse. The body must be embalmed or preserved, sealed in a hermetic impermeable coffin with absorbent material inside an outer case to the satisfaction of the doctor designated by the Minister of Public Works and Public Health, labelled, and accompanied by the medical/death statement, the embalming statement and a transport statement for the authorities of the destination. Exhumed remains travel in a hermetically sealed coffin with the exhumation permit where required. Typical delay is not published; ask the funeral home.
AW.authority: Directie Volksgezondheid (Ministry of Public Health) and the Civil Registry (Burgerlijke Stand), Aruba

documents: Death certificate from the country of death, with translation (confirm with consulate)
Embalming certificate (expected; confirm)
Certificate that the death was not caused by a contagious disease (expected; confirm)
Zinc sealing certificate (expected; confirm)
Export permit from the country of death
Passport of the deceased
AZ.coffin: Not published officially for entry. International practice requires a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin in an outer wooden case; confirm with the Azerbaijani consulate.
AZ.embalming: Not published officially for entry; embalming is expected for international transport. Confirm with the Azerbaijani consulate.
AZ.consular: Azerbaijan is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Contact the Azerbaijani embassy or consulate in the country of death about consular certification, legalisation or apostille and Azerbaijani translations. Local authorities do not work in English.
AZ.arrival: Not published officially. Expect customs clearance at the arrival airport (normally Baku) and handover to a local funeral service; confirm with the consulate. There are no cremation facilities in Azerbaijan. Local authorities must be told of infectious conditions such as hepatitis or HIV.
AZ.private_aviation: No official rule specific to human remains on private aircraft was found. Plan arrival at an international airport with customs, border and sanitary-quarantine control, and have the handling agent confirm clearance of the coffin in advance.
AZ.export: All foreign nationals who die in Azerbaijan undergo a compulsory autopsy, usually within 24 hours, by the district Medical Court Examination Department, which issues the AZS-106 medical death certificate. The death certificate (in Azerbaijani) is then issued by the district Registration Department or ASAN Service; no burial or repatriation is possible without it. Repatriation needs the death certificate, permission to remove the body from the coroner, the passport, and (for British nationals) a no-objection letter from their embassy.
AZ.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan (consular service); Medical Court Examination Department and Registration Department / ASAN Service for deaths in Azerbaijan

documents: Application for the BiH certificate for the transfer of human remains (laissez-passer), filled in by the next of kin
Formal shipment request from the funeral director
Ministry of Health transport request form for the burial location: Federation of BiH, Republika Srpska or Brcko District
Certified copies of the death certificate (Oslo embassy: medical certificate of death and court death certificate)
Certificate of no contagious disease (Chicago consulate: notarised letter from the health department)
Embalmer's affidavits (Chicago consulate: two notarised copies)
Acceptance letter from a BiH funeral home / proof of a funeral place reservation in BiH
Passport of the deceased (or birth and citizenship certificates if no valid passport)
Funeral director's letter with the flight itinerary
Funeral director's statement that the remains are prepared to international rules and the casket contains only the deceased
Police or local authority clearance to remove the body from the country of death (required by the Oslo embassy)
Consular fee receipt
BA.coffin: Hermetically sealed, metal-lined (zinc) casket, placed in an air tray for air transport (BiH Consulate General Chicago; BiH Embassy Oslo requires a hermetically sealed zinc coffin certified by the funeral home). No witnessing of the sealing by BiH officials abroad is published; the funeral director certifies the preparation.
BA.embalming: Embalming is expected: the BiH Consulate General in Chicago requires two notarised embalmer's affidavits. Within BiH embalming is not mandatory but can be requested, especially for repatriation (UK guidance).
BA.consular: The BiH embassy or consulate covering the place of death issues the laissez-passer / certificate for the transfer of human remains. Chicago fee: USD 30 plus USD 20 postage; Oslo charges per the consular tariff. For non-citizens, deaths from a contagious disease or exhumed remains, the certificate is issued only after approval by the competent BiH authorities (Oslo embassy), and a certified translation of the medical certificate of death into Bosnian, Croatian or Serbian is required.
BA.arrival: Customs and sanitary clearance at the arrival airport (Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Mostar or Tuzla). The BiH funeral home named in the acceptance letter collects the casket. No statutory burial deadline is published.
BA.private_aviation: No rules specific to private flights are published. The consulate needs the funeral home's letter with the flight itinerary before issuing the laissez-passer, so the private flight must be planned first; land at an airport with customs and sanitary inspection and have the BiH funeral home meet the aircraft.
BA.export: Leaving BiH: the death is registered with the local registry office (death certificate 'Smrtni list'; the cause of death is on the 'Potvrda o smrti' from the hospital or pathologist). The funeral director handles the documents, including the local death certificate, permission to remove the body and the deceased's passport. A post mortem may be carried out if the death was unknown, unnatural, sudden or violent. Embalming is not mandatory but can be requested. There are no crematoria in BiH (UK guidance: cremation takes place in Belgrade). Confirm sealing and export permit details with the funeral director and the destination consulate.
BA.authority: BiH embassies and consulates (laissez-passer); entity ministries of health (Federation of BiH, Republika Srpska, Brcko District)

documents: Death certificate (original and copy)
Passport of the deceased (original and copy)
Death notification or medical report
Police report, autopsy report or case papers if the death was accidental
Copy of the accompanying person's passport or residence ID, with contact number
Contact details of close family in Bangladesh
Name and phone number of the person receiving the body at the airport in Bangladesh
For migrant workers: proof the deceased's dues were paid (Dubai checklist)
NOC issued by the Bangladesh mission
BD.coffin: The official sources we reviewed give no coffin specification for entry. Confirm the coffin type with the Bangladesh mission and the airline.
BD.embalming: The official sources we reviewed (Bangladesh Consulate General in Dubai) do not mention embalming for entry. Embalming rules depend on the departure country and the airline; confirm with the Bangladesh mission.
BD.consular: The Bangladesh embassy or consulate issues the NOC free of charge. The Dubai consulate, for example, issues it the same day. The sponsor, employer (partner, manager, PRO or employee) or relatives can apply. For migrant workers, the Dubai consulate also requires proof that the deceased's dues were fully paid to the nominee. Requirements differ between missions, so check the checklist of the mission in the country of death.
BD.arrival: The remains are handed over at the airport to the receiving person named in the NOC application. Muslim burials in Bangladesh normally take place on the day of death or the next day, so families arrange burial immediately after arrival.
BD.private_aviation: No official guidance on private flights carrying remains was found. Use an international airport with customs and health staff, hold the mission's NOC and the receiver's details, and confirm aircraft landing permission and airport handling with operations.
BD.export: To take a body from Bangladesh, you need: a death certificate from a doctor or hospital, the passport, an embalming certificate and a permit to transfer the body (both usually arranged by a local funeral director), and a letter of no objection from the destination country's mission (e.g. the British High Commission in Dhaka). The formalities normally take 2 to 3 working days. A post-mortem may be held for unnatural, sudden or violent deaths, and a police investigation can delay release.
BD.authority: Bangladesh embassy/consulate (NOC); Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Bangladesh

documents: Laissez-passer for a corpse from the departure country's competent authority
Death certificate
Certificate of non-contagious disease
Embalming certificate where required by the departure country
BE.coffin: Strasbourg states (art. 6): impervious coffin with absorbent material, either a wooden outer coffin with sides at least 20 mm thick and a carefully soldered zinc inner coffin, or a single wooden coffin at least 30 mm thick lined with zinc; for air transport a purifying device (or resistance guarantees accepted by the departure state) is needed. Germany and other non-agreement countries (Regent's Decree of 20 June 1947): hermetically soldered metal coffin with about 5 cm of absorbent material and antiseptic, inside a wooden coffin at least 3 cm thick with watertight joints, screws no more than 20 cm apart and metal hoops.
BE.embalming: No Belgian embalming requirement for incoming bodies was found; follow the departure country's rules. For bodies leaving Belgium, an embalming certificate is part of the usual file.
BE.consular: From Strasbourg or Berlin agreement states the laissez-passer is sufficient. From other countries, ask the Belgian embassy or consulate whether a legalised or apostilled death certificate is needed.
BE.arrival: The receiving Belgian funeral director handles the formalities with the municipality for the burial or cremation; confirm the local requirements with the funeral director, as funeral rules are set by the regions (Brussels, Flanders, Wallonia).
BE.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
BE.export: A transfer licence is issued by the federal public health ministry (FPS Public Health, Belgium's declared Strasbourg authority) on the basis of the death certificate and a medical certificate stating the body has no infectious disease. The coffin is sealed and verified by the police or a municipal officer, and an embalming certificate is normally provided; all documents travel with the coffin. The US Embassy notes that remains cannot ordinarily be sent before the third or fourth working day after death.
BE.authority: FPS Public Health (federal); municipality of burial

documents: Death certificate issued by the local authorities and legalised by the Bulgarian embassy or consulate (or a death certificate issued by the embassy)
Transport or export permit of the country of death
Embalming certificate where required by the departure country
Funeral director's sealing certificate
Proof that all costs are paid (deposit with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or payment document from relatives or insurer)
BG.coffin: Bulgarian rules for incoming coffins are not published separately. For bodies leaving Bulgaria, Ordinance No. 2 of 2011 (art. 24) requires a hermetically sealed metal coffin with a filtering system, or a solid wooden coffin lined with sheet metal that is soldered and sealed, or a tightly closed transport container, with sawdust and a chlorine biocide or an absorbent mattress at the bottom. Confirm the standard for entry with the Bulgarian consulate and the airline.
BG.embalming: No Bulgarian requirement is published for incoming bodies; follow the departure country's and airline's rules. Ordinance No. 2 of 2011 (art. 23) allows embalming and/or cooling (maximum 8 C inside the container) for long-distance transport. For bodies leaving Bulgaria, the UK FCDO lists an embalming certificate among the repatriation documents.
BG.consular: The Bulgarian embassy or consulate in the country of death legalises the local death certificate or issues its own, and assists with the transfer of the coffin or urn once relatives or an insurer have paid all costs. The municipality of the deceased's permanent address then issues the Bulgarian death certificate on the basis of the document accompanying the body.
BG.arrival: Not published in detail: arrival health and customs formalities should be confirmed with the receiving Bulgarian funeral director and the Bulgarian consulate. Funeral arrangements follow the will of the deceased or, failing that, the spouse, adult children, parents or siblings.
BG.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
BG.export: Leaving Bulgaria: transport abroad requires a permit from the director of the competent Regional Health Inspectorate (RZI), on the model in annex 2 of Ordinance No. 2 of 21 April 2011. The coffin (hermetically sealed metal coffin with filtering system, or sheet-metal-lined wooden coffin soldered and sealed, or closed transport container) is closed in the presence of a state health inspector of the RZI. Transport is by specialised funeral vehicle only. Deaths from cholera, plague, typhus, typhoid, anthrax, infectious tuberculosis, CCHF, polio or a new dangerous infectious disease require sealed polyethylene bags inside a sheet-metal-lined coffin. The UK FCDO lists a local death certificate, an embalming certificate and a certificate permitting transfer of the remains.
BG.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Bulgarian missions abroad; municipalities; Regional Health Inspectorates (RZI) for export

documents: Request letter from the deceased's family with contact details of the person accompanying the body and of the relatives receiving it in Bahrain
Copy of the deceased's passport
Death certificate legalised by the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the country of death
Embalming and sealing certificates as required by the departure country and airline (confirm with the embassy)
BH.coffin: No Bahraini import standard is published. Use a hermetically sealed casket in an outer case meeting airline requirements; confirm with the Bahraini embassy.
BH.embalming: Remains leaving Bahrain need an embalming and sealing certificate (gov.uk). Incoming embalming rules are not published; confirm with the embassy.
BH.consular: Bahraini embassy or consulate (Ministry of Foreign Affairs service, with the Ministry of Health as cooperating entity; legal basis Decree No. 4 of 1971) handles the transfer file in 3 working days, arranges the flight with the airline and informs the Ministry. Bahrain is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
BH.arrival: Under the MOFA service, the Ministry of Health arranges transport from the airport and the relatives named in the application receive the body. Arrival customs formalities are not published; confirm with the handling agent. Under Islamic law burial takes place as soon as possible. Cremation is possible at the Hindu Cremation Ground in Askar.
BH.private_aviation: No official rule specific to private or charter flights carrying human remains was found. Arrive at Bahrain International Airport with the handling agent confirming customs and health clearance in advance, and check current airspace and flight status before departure.
BH.export: Required: death certificate (attested at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs), notification of cause of death, embalming and sealing certificate, police transfer of dead body certificate, cancelled passport and the home embassy's no-objection letter. The body must be identified by someone who knew the deceased. Release can follow within a day of the no-objection letter; repatriation normally takes 7 to 10 days.
BH.authority: Bahrain Ministry of Foreign Affairs (embassies), with the Ministry of Health; police (exit)

documents: Death certificate from the country of death
Medical certificate of cause of death or non-contagious disease certificate (as required by the departure country)
Embalming or conservation certificate where required by the departure country
Entry authorisation from the French embassy or consulate
Name of the receiving funeral home
BL.coffin: For air transport an airtight coffin (metal box) is mandatory under French rules. Confirm the exact coffin specification with the French consulate and the funeral homes.
BL.embalming: France does not impose a single rule for incoming bodies; embalming or conservation care is normally required by the departure country and by carriers. Confirm with the consulate.
BL.consular: The French embassy or consulate in the country of death authorises entry of the body into French territory; the funeral home handles the procedures. France is a party to the Strasbourg Agreement; whether a laissez-passer from another party state is accepted for Saint-Barthelemy should be confirmed with the consulate. Families bear all costs (insurance may cover them).
BL.arrival: The receiving funeral home takes charge at the airport and arranges the funeral; confirm local burial or cremation deadlines with it. Transport from the collectivity to mainland France is authorised by the representative of the State in the collectivity, and transport from mainland France to the collectivity by the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed.
BL.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long and heavy once metal-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin). Saint-Barthelemy airport has a very short runway restricted to small aircraft, so most jets cannot land there; plan a transfer via a larger nearby airport and confirm aircraft suitability with operations. The French airtight coffin rule applies to any air transport.
BL.export: To send a body out of French territory, the funeral home obtains authorisation from the State's representative (prefect) for the place where the coffin is closed; for this collectivity confirm the competent State representative locally. An airtight coffin (metal box) is mandatory for air transport, and the destination country's consular requirements also apply.
BL.authority: French embassy or consulate abroad (entry); State representative, prefect delegate for Saint-Barthelemy and Saint-Martin (exit)

documents: Medical statement from the competent doctor where the death occurred, or an extract of the death certificate (name, birth date/age, date and place of death, cause of death or statement that death was natural / not due to a contagious disease)
Statement from the person who embalmed or otherwise preserved the body, describing the method used
Statement from the competent authority of the place of death on how and by which route the body will be transported (transfer permit)
BQ.coffin: Hermetically sealed coffin made of impermeable material (zinc-lined in practice) with absorbent material, containing only the body, its clothing, packing material and personal effects, packed to the satisfaction of the doctor designated by the island executive council (bestuurscollege) in a well-closing outer coffin. Name, first names, date of birth, date and place of death and destination must be clearly marked on the coffin. The law does not say who must witness the sealing at origin.
BQ.embalming: Required: the body must be embalmed or properly preserved by another method. If the death was due to a quarantinable disease, arterial and cavity embalming is mandatory.
BQ.consular: No specific consular step is set by the law; the transport statement must come from the competent authority of the country of death. Confirm with the receiving funeral home whether legalisation, apostille or translation of the foreign documents is needed.
BQ.arrival: Documents are presented on arrival; customs and the health authority clear the coffin. Bodies brought into Caribbean Netherlands must be buried as soon as possible and only with free written leave from the civil registrar (ambtenaar van de burgerlijke stand), which cannot be issued before the death statement is produced.
BQ.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private aircraft. Fly into an airport with customs and health clearance (Bonaire Flamingo, Sint Eustatius or Saba; the Saba and Sint Eustatius runways are short and limit aircraft size). The same coffin and document rules apply as for cargo.
BQ.export: Leaving Caribbean Netherlands: the same rules apply in reverse. The body must be embalmed or preserved, sealed in a hermetic impermeable coffin with absorbent material inside an outer case to the satisfaction of the doctor designated by the island executive council (bestuurscollege), labelled, and accompanied by the medical/death statement, the embalming statement and a transport statement for the authorities of the destination. Exhumed remains travel in a hermetically sealed coffin with the exhumation and transport permit where the country requires one and a death certificate extract. Typical delay is not published; confirm with the local funeral home.
BQ.authority: Island executive council (bestuurscollege) of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius or Saba and the civil registrar

documents: Local death certificate (confirm apostille or legalisation with the Brazilian consulate)
Conservation record (Ata de Conservacao de Restos Mortais Humanos) or equivalent embalming certificate, attached by the carrier to the transport documents (RDC 662/2022 Art. 6)
Certificate that the death was not caused by a contagious disease (usually asked by consulates; to confirm)
Transit or removal permit from the country of death
Passport of the deceased and air waybill
BR.coffin: RDC 662/2022 defines the funeral urn as an outer wooden box lined inside with zinc sheets or an equivalent material, impermeable and without a viewing window. The ANVISA conservation record model states the remains are placed in the impermeable urn which is then sealed in front of the signatories (family representative, doctor, assistant and two witnesses).
BR.embalming: Mandatory: remains must have undergone a conservation procedure (formalinisation, embalming or another method set by ANVISA or the Ministry of Health), recorded in a conservation record (RDC 662/2022 Art. 5 and 6). Conservation and transfer services are prohibited when death was caused by spongiform encephalitis, haemorrhagic fever or another new infectious disease designated by WHO and the Ministry of Health (Art. 8).
BR.consular: Brazilian consulates can register the death and advise on the documents for the transfer; the exact list (including any apostille or translation) varies by consulate, so confirm with the consulate in the country of death. Brazil is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Repatriation costs are normally borne by the family or insurer.
BR.arrival: ANVISA carries out sanitary control of remains at airports only in public health emergencies or risk situations (Art. 3), but the documents must be available whenever requested (Art. 4). A Brazilian funeral company receives the urn, clears customs and arranges burial or cremation under municipal rules. Ashes are not subject to sanitary control.
BR.private_aviation: RDC 662/2022 Art. 5 requires human remains to travel in the cargo compartment of the means of transport. Many business jets have no hold able to take a zinc-lined coffin, so check with the operator and ANVISA (port, airport and border health service at the arrival airport) before booking: the casket travels in the cargo hold, usually of an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650. Keep the conservation record and all documents on board.
BR.export: A Brazilian funeral company arranges conservation (embalming or formalinisation) with the ANVISA conservation record, the zinc-lined urn, the notary-issued death certificate and a Federal Police authorisation document, and meets the destination country's consular requirements. Autopsy results can take a few weeks and cremation needs a judge's approval.
BR.authority: ANVISA (port, airport and border health control); Brazilian consulates abroad

documents: Certified copy of the death certificate
Permission of the Minister of Health to land the body, obtained through a Bahamian funeral home
Embalming certificate or embalmer's statement (usually requested; not on the official sheet consulted)
Export or transit permit from the country of death
BS.coffin: Hermetically sealed casket required. No witnessed sealing requirement was found.
BS.embalming: Not stated on the official sheet consulted, but embalming is normally expected; confirm with the Bahamian funeral home.
BS.consular: No consular visa was found as a requirement. The Bahamas High Commission in London advises the sending undertaker to liaise directly with a Bahamian mortician, who obtains the approvals from the Ministry of Health (Chief Medical Officer).
BS.arrival: The Bahamian funeral home presents the Ministry of Health approval and the documents and collects the casket. Burial timing follows the funeral home and local rules.
BS.private_aviation: Private flights must land at a Bahamian airport of entry with customs and immigration (for example Nassau). The Ministry of Health permission must be obtained before arrival; no specific private-aviation rule for remains was found.
BS.export: Leaving The Bahamas, the death is registered with the Registrar General's Department (certificates are usually issued within a few days); after a sudden or unnatural death, a post-mortem at the Rand Morgue (Nassau) usually takes 4 to 6 working days for foreign nationals. The funeral home then provides the death certificate, an embalming certificate and a certificate permitting transfer of the remains.
BS.authority: Ministry of Health (Chief Medical Officer), The Bahamas

documents: Import permit from the Minister (Ministry of Health), obtained before arrival
Medical certificate of the cause of death (or certified copy)
Death certificate
Deceased's passport
Certificate that the death was not from a contagious/epidemic disease
Embalming certificate
Conveyance of dead bodies form
Burial order from the family
Import/export permit from the Botswana Unified Revenue Service (BURS), depending on the country (government statement, 2023)
BW.coffin: Section 6 of the Act requires a body not in cold storage that is to remain unburied for a period risking offence to be placed in a strong hermetically sealed sheet-metal shell inside a stout wooden coffin, or else carefully embalmed. Exhumed remains must be sealed in a sheet-metal shell in a stout wooden coffin before removal. The permit may impose further conditions.
BW.embalming: An embalming certificate is among the documents the Ministry of Foreign Affairs says families may be asked for (statement to Parliament, December 2023). The Act accepts embalming as an alternative to a sealed metal shell for keeping bodies.
BW.consular: The permit application is addressed to the Minister. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, through Botswana's missions, assists families of Batswana who die abroad; the family must appoint a local representative in the country of death, and the documents requested depend on that country.
BW.arrival: Customs clearance (BURS permit) and health checks on arrival; a local undertaker collects. Exhumed remains can only be imported at least 2 years after burial (4 years for infectious disease deaths). Ashes do not need a permit.
BW.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A casket on a private aircraft should arrive at an international airport with customs and health (port health) officers, with landing permission arranged through a local handling agent, and the original documents travelling with the casket. The ministerial import permit must be obtained before the body enters Botswana, whatever the type of flight.
BW.export: Removal from Botswana also needs a permit from the Minister, with the cause-of-death certificate and written approval from the authorities of the destination country. UK guidance lists death certificate, passport copy, embalming certificate and a certificate permitting transfer. Deaths should be registered within 30 days; certificates are in English.
BW.authority: Minister of Health (Conveyance of Dead Bodies Act, Cap. 65:01); BURS for customs

documents: Death certificate (translated into English or French if needed), ideally stating the cause of death
If no death certificate: other evidence such as a coroner's letter identifying the remains, reviewed by a quarantine officer
Embalming certificate and transit permit as required by the country of departure
Air waybill or flight documents
CA.coffin: At minimum a leak-proof container (CBSA memorandum D19-9-3); some carriers require a hermetically sealed container. If the death certificate does not state the cause of death or shows a communicable disease, a hermetically sealed container can usually be released with an advisory not to open it; otherwise the CBSA officer must contact a quarantine officer. No witnessed sealing is required by Canada.
CA.embalming: Not addressed by the federal import rules. The country of departure and airlines usually require it; provincial rules govern later handling.
CA.consular: The CBSA memorandum sets no consular, legalisation or import-permit step for entry; documents in other languages need an English or French translation. Confirm any carrier or provincial requirements with the receiving Canadian funeral director.
CA.arrival: CBSA border services officers check the documents and release the remains, referring to a PHAC quarantine officer if there is no death certificate, a communicable disease is suspected, the cause of death is missing with an unsealed container, or the remains arrive damaged. A Canadian funeral director collects and obtains the provincial burial or cremation permit; timing follows provincial rules.
CA.private_aviation: Private aircraft arriving from abroad must land at a CBSA-designated airport of entry and report to the CBSA before passengers or goods leave the aircraft. The remains must be declared on arrival with the death certificate; the same Quarantine Act screening applies. Confirm reporting procedures with the CBSA for the chosen airport.
CA.export: The funeral home obtains the provincial death registration and burial or transit permit, embalms and caskets the body as the destination requires, and meets the destination consulate's requirements (ask whether an apostille or other authentication is needed). If the deceased had a communicable disease, prior permission from the Public Health Agency of Canada is required before export. Coroner investigations can delay release.
CA.authority: Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC), with screening by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA); provincial vital statistics authorities

documents: Death certificate (confirm legalisation and translation needs with the DR Congo consulate)
Embalming certificate
Certificate that death was not due to a contagious disease (usual practice; confirm with the consulate)
Permit for corpse transportation from the DR Congo embassy or consulate
Copy of the deceased's passport; if no valid Congolese passport, the consulate issues a substitute document (tenant-lieu)
CD.coffin: Not officially published for entry. In practice, a hermetically sealed (zinc- or metal-lined) casket in a wooden outer case is expected for international air transport. Confirm with the consulate.
CD.embalming: Embalming is standard for international transport. The rules for entry are not officially published.
CD.consular: The DR Congo Embassy in Washington lists a 'permit for corpse transportation': USD 100 if the deceased has a valid passport, USD 150 if a tenant-lieu travel document must be created. Payment is by money order. Other missions charge their own fees. DR Congo is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
CD.arrival: Customs and health clearance procedures at Kinshasa N'djili are not officially published. The family or a local funeral home collects the casket. Mortuary standards vary, and cold storage is limited outside Kinshasa.
CD.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A private aircraft carrying a casket must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services; have the local handling agent and receiving funeral home confirm in advance that the remains can be cleared from a private flight.
CD.export: The local funeral home, working with an international funeral director, obtains a civil-registry death certificate, an embalming certificate and a certificate giving permission to transfer the body abroad. After a violent or sudden death, a certificate of identification is issued by the judicial police and district prosecutor, and the attorney general may order an autopsy without family consent. Routine cases are usually released within a few days; deaths under investigation can take more than a month. Few local undertakers can quickly supply international caskets. Cremation is not available in the DRC.
CD.authority: DR Congo embassy or consulate in the country of death; DR Congo health and customs services on arrival

documents: Copy of the deceased's birth certificate
Proof of Congolese citizenship (passport, national ID or citizenship certificate)
Hospital medical record certifying the death and its cause
Funeral home letter confirming it handles the shipment to the Republic of Congo
Funeral home certificate that the body was embalmed under local sanitary rules and poses no health threat
Copy of the funeral home's licence
Signed letter from the family representative to the Ambassador, with a copy of their photo ID
Flight reservation or itinerary for the remains
Prepaid tracked return envelope (when applying by mail)
CG.coffin: Not specified by the embassy. A hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin in an outer wooden case is the usual international standard; confirm with the embassy and the airline.
CG.embalming: Required: the embassy asks for a funeral home certificate that the body was embalmed and poses no health risk.
CG.consular: The Congolese embassy or consulate in the country of death issues the authorisation for the transfer of human remains. The Washington embassy states 5 to 7 business days from receipt, no express service, payment by money order or cash in person, fees non-refundable. Translators must be recognised by the Congolese authorities. Not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
CG.arrival: Arrival clearance at Brazzaville Maya-Maya or Pointe-Noire is not published; a local undertaker collects. No official burial deadline found.
CG.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. The embassy asks for the flight reservation or itinerary of the remains, so submit the charter details and confirm acceptance. Land at Brazzaville or Pointe-Noire with customs and health services, with the original documents travelling with the casket.
CG.export: Documents: hospital medical death certificate (several days), civil registry death certificate (French), certificate of identification and autopsy report from judicial police/prosecutor for sudden or violent deaths, certificate of embalming and permit to transfer, arranged through local and international undertakers. Translators must be recognised locally. Release usually within a few days; road deaths can take over a month. Cremation is available.
CG.authority: Embassy or consulate of the Republic of Congo in the country of death

documents: Laissez-passer (Leichenpass) from the departure country's competent authority
Death certificate (international or multilingual version where possible)
Funeral director's encoffining and sealing record
Embalming and non-contagion certificates where required by the departure country
CH.coffin: Strasbourg standard: an outer wooden coffin with a soldered inner zinc coffin, or a single zinc-lined wooden coffin, with absorbent material; the coffin may contain only the body and personal effects.
CH.embalming: No specific Swiss requirement for incoming bodies was found; follow the departure country's and airline's rules. Bodies leaving Switzerland usually travel with an embalming certificate.
CH.consular: From Strasbourg or Berlin states no consular step is normally needed. From other countries, ask the Swiss embassy or consulate whether legalised documents are required. Switzerland's declared treaty authority is the Federal Office of Public Health.
CH.arrival: Customs clearance at the arrival airport, then the receiving Swiss funeral director arranges burial or cremation with the canton and municipality; rules and deadlines vary by canton. Cremation is the norm in Switzerland.
CH.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside. Flights from EU countries also need Swiss customs clearance.
CH.export: Since 1 January 2025 the Leichenpass for a body leaving Switzerland is issued by the competent civil registry office (Zivilstandsamt), previously the cantonal doctor, based on an encoffining and sealing record from an authorised funeral director proving the coffin is sealed and contains only the deceased. The cantonal procedure varies (Aargau, Zug).
CH.authority: Federal Office of Public Health (treaty authority); cantonal civil registry offices

documents: Full copy of the death record (copie intégrale de l'acte de décès), for transcription into the Ivorian registers
Medical death certificate
Medical certificate of non-contagion
Certificate of non-epidemic
Embalming (soins de conservation) certificate
Coffining record (procès-verbal de mise en bière)
Authorisation to transport the body after coffining
Authorisation to close the coffin
Mortuary laissez-passer
Proof of identity: national ID card, ONECI identity attestation or valid passport
CI.coffin: The Ivorian consulate in Paris requires the coffining record and the authorisation to close the coffin. From France, a hermetic metal-lined coffin is mandatory for air transport. No Ivorian technical specification for the coffin is published.
CI.embalming: Required: the Ivorian consulate in Paris asks for an embalming (soins de conservation) certificate.
CI.consular: The Ivorian consulate general issues the autorisation de transfert de corps. The funeral home prepares the file and lodges it at the consulate; a consular card is not required; chancery fee EUR 10 (Ivorian embassy in Paris). Processing time is not published. Côte d'Ivoire is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement, so a mortuary laissez-passer alone is not enough.
CI.arrival: Customs and health clearance at Abidjan Félix-Houphouët-Boigny airport is not officially documented. The family or an Ivorian funeral home collects the casket. Cremation is not permitted in Côte d'Ivoire.
CI.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A private aircraft carrying a casket must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services; have the local handling agent and receiving funeral home confirm in advance that the remains can be cleared from a private flight.
CI.export: UK government guidance lists these documents for taking a body out of Côte d'Ivoire: a death certificate, a transfer authorisation, permission to remove the body issued by a coroner, and authorisation from the Ministry of Interior. The police can order an autopsy without the family's consent, often as soon as the body reaches the morgue. Cremation is not permitted. Typical delays are not published. From France: the funeral company files the request; the transport is authorised by the préfet of the département where the coffin is closed, and a hermetic metal-lined coffin is mandatory for air transport (service-public.gouv.fr). Because this country is not a party to the Berlin (1937) or Strasbourg (1973) agreements, the prefecture may also ask for a certificate of non-epidemic (CNE) issued by the regional health agency (ARS).
CI.authority: Ivorian consulates abroad (entry); Ministry of Interior (exit)

documents: Certified death certificate stating the cause of death, in English (expected; not listed in the Act)
Embalming certificate (embalming is legally required)
Casket sealing certificate from the funeral director (expected)
Written exemption from the Secretary of Health if burial cannot take place within 48 hours of arrival
CK.coffin: Section 44 of the Public Health Act 2004: remains must be kept encased in a sealed and impervious container at all times while held or transported in the Cook Islands. Land burial must be in a sealed and impervious crypt (section 46). Who witnesses the sealing is not specified.
CK.embalming: Required by law: remains brought in must be kept embalmed until burial or cremation (section 44).
CK.consular: No consular transfer permit is set out in the Act. Most repatriations come from New Zealand (Cook Islanders are NZ citizens); the Cook Islands High Commission in Wellington and Consulate in Auckland can advise.
CK.arrival: Burial or cremation must take place within 48 hours of the remains being brought into the Cook Islands (section 44), unless the Secretary of Health issues a written exemption with conditions (section 45). Where infection with a notifiable condition is suspected, the medical officer may direct special handling (section 86). The family or funeral director collects at Rarotonga.
CK.private_aviation: Rarotonga International Airport is the port of entry. No rule specific to private flights carrying remains was found; the 48-hour burial clock starts when the remains are brought into the Cook Islands (section 44), including when burial is on an outer island, so the funeral and any domestic connection must be ready before landing.
CK.export: Remains received in the Cook Islands must be buried or cremated within 24 hours, or, if they are to be buried or cremated elsewhere, embalmed and sealed in an impervious container within 24 hours and transported out of the Cook Islands within 48 hours of receipt (section 43), unless the Secretary of Health grants a written exemption (section 45).
CK.authority: Te Marae Ora, Ministry of Health (Secretary of Health), Cook Islands

documents: Death certificate, apostilled or legalised, with Spanish translation (to confirm with the consulate)
Health authority document from the place of origin stating the transport poses no public health risk, endorsed (visado) by the Chilean consul (Decree 357 Art. 78)
Embalming certificate (to confirm)
Authorisation of the competent SEREMI de Salud for international transport and entry (Art. 75)
Passport of the deceased (confirm with the consulate)
CL.coffin: Coffins used to transport bodies must be impermeable and able to be hermetically closed (Art. 67); burial in a vault or niche requires a hermetically sealed coffin (Art. 51). A metal-lined sealed coffin with an outer wooden case is the practical standard.
CL.embalming: Not expressly required for entry in the regulation; in practice expected for international transport. Bodies normally must be buried within 48 hours unless embalmed with health authority approval or a judicial or health order applies (Art. 48), so embalming matters for the timing in Chile.
CL.consular: Decree 357 requires the origin health documents to be endorsed by the Chilean consul. Chile has joined the Hague Apostille Convention, so ask the consulate whether an apostille now replaces the consular endorsement. Chile is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
CL.arrival: The SEREMI de Salud authorises the entry and transfer. Funeral homes may not change coffins or move bodies without health authority authorisation (Art. 66). A Chilean funeral home collects the coffin; burial needs the civil registry burial pass. Cremation needs SEREMI authorisation and, after an accident or suspected crime, judicial authorisation.
CL.private_aviation: Decree 357 Art. 77 requires a coffin moved between cities or abroad to travel in a separate compartment of the aircraft under the captain's responsibility. A coffin in the passenger cabin of a business jet may not satisfy this; check with the SEREMI de Salud and the operator. Land at an international airport with customs, police and health services.
CL.export: The SEREMI de Salud authorises international transport (Decree 357 Art. 75). The health authority checks that the coffin is impermeable and in good condition, draws up a record, seals the coffin and issues the authorisation; the seal may not be removed before arrival at destination (Art. 77). The civil registry death certificate is usually issued within 24 to 72 hours. If a judge is involved the body is released only when the judge is satisfied; straightforward cases take one to two weeks according to UK guidance.
CL.authority: Secretaria Regional Ministerial de Salud (SEREMI de Salud); Chilean consulates abroad

documents: Request letter addressed to the Ambassador / High Commissioner
Death certificate (English or French translation if needed)
Deceased's passport or Cameroonian ID, birth certificate
Embalming certificate
Free-from-infection certificate
Authorisation to remove the body from the country of death
Affidavit of contents (UK mission)
Burial permit and regional authorisation from the Service of Social and Cultural Affairs (Centre or Littoral), signed by the Prefect (UK mission)
Funeral company details, flight ticket copy if available (Germany mission)
CM.coffin: Not detailed by the missions whose pages were opened; confirm the casket specification with the mission and the airline. The UK mission asks for an affidavit of contents.
CM.consular: Certificate of Repatriation / mortuary laissez-passer issued by the Cameroonian mission; documents uploaded and fee paid online at evisacam.cm (Laissez-Passer section). Berlin embassy: fee EUR 153, non-refundable; apply at least 7 days before departure, indicative processing 7 days. The death certificate issued by the Tokyo embassy is free. Without the Prefect's regional authorisation the UK mission may not issue the certificate.
CM.arrival: Customs and health clearance at Douala or Yaounde-Nsimalen; the family or funeral home collects. The regional authorisation covers transfer into the region. No burial deadline published.
CM.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A casket on a private aircraft should arrive at an international airport with customs and health (port health) officers, with landing permission arranged through a local handling agent, and the original documents travelling with the casket. The consular Certificate of Repatriation and the regional authorisation must be obtained before departure.
CM.export: A funeral home obtains authorisation to repatriate the body. Needed: death certificate (after hospital registration), cause-of-death certificate (usually within a week), post-mortem report if death outside hospital, passport. Embalming offered by funeral homes. Autopsy reports can take long. UK guidance cites about GBP 2,000 for repatriation to the UK (estimate).
CM.authority: Cameroonian embassies/high commissions (Ministry of External Relations); Prefect of Centre or Littoral region

documents: Application filed by a relative, the consulate or the receiving unit, approved by the civil affairs, overseas Chinese affairs and foreign affairs authorities of the place of death, origin or burial
Corpse/coffin entry permit from the entry-exit inspection and quarantine authority (now under customs)
Death certificate and identity document of the deceased (confirm the exact list with the carrier)
Embalming and encoffining certificates (expected; confirm the current list)
Customs declaration of the remains
CN.coffin: No public text sets the casket specification; the casket is checked by border quarantine before release. Use a hermetically sealed casket to IATA standard and confirm with the designated carrier.
CN.embalming: No published Chinese rule sets embalming for incoming remains; it is expected for long-haul transport, so confirm with the designated carrier. Exit files from China include embalming, encoffining and quarantine certificates (Indian Embassy Beijing).
CN.consular: The Chinese embassy or consulate in the country of death advises on approvals and document legalisation. Approval comes from Chinese civil affairs and foreign affairs authorities; only the China Funeral Association's international body transport network and authorised funeral homes may carry out the transport.
CN.arrival: Customs releases the remains only on the quarantine permit. The designated carrier or funeral home collects the casket. Cremation is the general rule in many areas; burial follows local funeral reform rules.
CN.private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights found. The remains must still go through border quarantine and customs at an international port, with the designated carrier involved; foreign private aircraft also need CAAC permits.
CN.export: For foreigners: the hospital issues the death certificate (or a forensic certificate for unnatural deaths), and the public security exit-entry bureau issues a foreigner's death certificate when the body will go abroad. Notarisation and authentication follow if required. Only the China Funeral Association's international network and authorised funeral homes (three in Shanghai) handle repatriation; they embalm, encoff and obtain quarantine and exit permits. The Indian Embassy in Beijing reports about 25-30 days for natural deaths and about 45 days for unnatural deaths.
CN.authority: Ministry of Civil Affairs / China Funeral Association international body transport service centre; General Administration of Customs (border quarantine)

documents: Death certificate (apostille and Spanish translation advisable; not spelled out in Resolution 717, confirm with the consulate)
Certificate from the Colombian cemetery or crematorium stating place, municipality, date and expected time of burial or cremation
Record of preservation, packaging and transfer (acta de preservacion, embalaje y traslado, Annex 3) with the transport responsibility manifest naming airline/operator, flight and destination
Copy of the applicant's identity document
Entry/exit document review form (Annex 7), signed by the health authority at the point of entry
CO.coffin: Resolution 717 (art. 27): a non-reusable first coffin in direct contact with the body, impermeable, leak- and odour-proof and hermetically closed (sealed with plastic or rubber adhesive, or a welded or fused metal lining), with absorbent material sprayed with antiseptic; an optional second hermetic coffin depending on airline requirements; outer packaging compliant with ISPM 15 (ICA Resolution 1079 of 2004). No witness for the sealing is required by the text.
CO.embalming: Mandatory: every body transported by air must undergo thanatopraxy (embalming) (Resolution 717, arts. 21 and 26), performed by a qualified thanatopractor. Substances that are dangerous goods under ICAO rules, or whose concentration or volume endangers air safety, are prohibited. Ashes in an urn need no health requirement beyond the cremation certificate.
CO.consular: Colombian consulates advise families (Decree 869 of 2016 limits the Foreign Ministry's role to advice and assistance); no consular transfer permit is listed in Resolution 717. The state has no budget for repatriation (the Foreign Ministry cites USD 10,000 to 30,000 and recommends travel insurance); ashes may in some cases be sent by diplomatic bag. Colombia is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
CO.arrival: At the point of entry the departmental, district or municipal health authority checks the documents and signs the 'formato de revision documental de cadaveres en puntos de entrada y salida' (Resolution 717, art. 50 and Annex 7); the acta de preservacion, embalaje y traslado must be shown to the port/airport health authorities (art. 49). A Colombian funeral home collects the coffin and obtains the burial or cremation licence. Resolution 717 gives operators 12 months (to April 2027) to comply fully.
CO.private_aviation: Resolution 717 applies to all air transport: the funeral provider must coordinate safety requirements with the air operator and comply with the Colombian Aeronautical Regulations (RAC), and the manifest names the carrier and flight. Land at an international airport with a health authority presence (for example Bogota El Dorado) so the document check can be signed; arrange for the receiving funeral home to meet the aircraft with all originals.
CO.export: Formal identification by the Instituto Nacional de Medicina Legal comes first (weeks, or months if DNA is needed), and the Fiscalia (prosecutor) must confirm release. The Registraduria death certificate is usually ready in about 2 days and should be apostilled by the Foreign Ministry. The funeral home embalms the body (mandatory for air), packs it per Resolution 717 art. 27, completes the acta de preservacion, embalaje y traslado and manifest, and presents the death certificate, cemetery/crematorium certificate of destination and applicant ID to the health authority at the exit airport, which signs the Annex 7 form. Cremation requires prosecutor authorisation and is only possible for natural deaths or after a full autopsy.
CO.authority: Ministry of Health and Social Protection (Resolution 717 of 2026); departmental, district or municipal health authorities at points of entry; Colombian consulates (advice)

documents: Official death certificate stating the cause of death, issued by the civil registry of the place of death
Declaration by the person who prepared the body stating the method of preparation (embalming certificate), certified by the competent authority
Sworn statement that the coffin contains only the remains of the deceased
Transit permit with the name, surname and age of the deceased, issued by the authority of the place of death
Passport or ID of the deceased; apostille and official Spanish translation for any later registration of the death in Costa Rica
