CR.coffin: Executive Decree No. 1 (La Gaceta 69, 22 March 1968) requires the body to be placed in an impermeable coffin that is hermetically closed; for air transport the coffin travels in the hold of a passenger or cargo aircraft and may be fitted with a safety valve. The coffin must carry a fixed plate showing name, age, sex and final destination, and copies of the documents travel with it. Note: Costa Rica's General Cemetery Regulation (Decree 32833-S, art. 30) prohibits in-ground burial in metal coffins or other slowly decomposing materials, so a zinc-lined shipping casket may need to be replaced or placed in a vault or niche; ask the cemetery.
CR.embalming: Required: the 1968 decree states that the body must be adequately embalmed. Costa Rica also requires an embalming certificate to send a body abroad (Decree 32833-S, art. 67).
CR.consular: No published consular visa of the documents was found. Costa Rica is an Apostille party; to register the death of a Costa Rican abroad with the Civil Registry (TSE) the foreign death certificate must be apostilled or authenticated and translated by an official translator. Confirm with the Costa Rican consulate whether it wants to see the shipping documents before departure.
CR.arrival: Customs and health clearance at the arrival airport (San Jose or Liberia), with the receiving funeral home collecting the coffin. Burial must take place 24-36 hours after death unless the Ministry of Health area office (Area Rectora de Salud) grants a written extension (Decree 32833-S, art. 29 as amended by Decree 42474-S); the funeral home should request this extension for a repatriated body.
CR.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the originals travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once sealed) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Costa Rican rules allow the sealed coffin on a passenger or cargo aircraft; no specific rule for private flights was found. Land at an international airport with customs and health officers (Juan Santamaria, San Jose, or Daniel Oduber, Liberia).
CR.export: Leaving Costa Rica: international transport needs prior authorisation from the Ministry of Health area office (Area Rectora de Salud) on: a written request by a direct relative (or the embassy for a foreigner) stating destination and route; the Civil Registry death declaration form; a sworn statement that the coffin contains only the deceased; a medical stamp and a Red Cross stamp; and an embalming certificate (Decree 32833-S, art. 67). The 1968 decree requires embalming and a hermetically closed impermeable coffin. An official autopsy is carried out when a body is to be sent abroad, except for an obviously natural death of a person over 75 (FCDO). A temporary death certificate is issued first; violent or suspicious deaths involve the OIJ and a judge.
CR.authority: Ministry of Health (Area Rectora de Salud); Civil Registry (Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones)

documents: Consular transcription of the death (Transcripcion de la Defuncion)
Medical certificate that the body was embalmed according to the stipulated measures, with official Spanish translation
Burial licence from the authorities of the country of death, with official Spanish translation
Document from the health ministry of the country of death authorising the transfer, with official Spanish translation
Consular declaration that the body is prepared according to the stipulated measures
CU.coffin: The Cuban consulate certifies that the body is prepared according to the stipulated measures; the exact casket specification is not published on the page consulted. Use a hermetically sealed coffin and confirm with the consulate.
CU.embalming: Required: a medical certificate that the body was embalmed according to the stipulated measures.
CU.consular: Each document and its Spanish translation is authenticated by the foreign ministry of the country of death (in Canada, Global Affairs Canada) and then legalised by the Cuban consulate. Fees vary by consulate: the Cuban consulates in Canada charge CAD 256 per document (each original and each translation) plus CAD 176 for the declaration on the preparation of the body, while the Cuban consular fee list in Mexico shows body transfer and death transcription as free, stating that every procedure linked to the death of a Cuban citizen is exempt. Other Cuban consulates advise families to contact the nearest consulate directly.
CU.arrival: The family contacts the Funeraria de Calzada y K in Havana with the name, date and cause of death, the person in Cuba responsible for the body and the cemetery of burial. Customs and health clearance on arrival are handled with the funeral service; timing was not found officially.
CU.private_aviation: No official rule for remains on private flights was found. Private flights must land at a Cuban international airport with customs and health; flights from the United States are subject to US sanctions and export-control rules, which must be checked before planning.
CU.export: In Cuba, the local funeral director registers the death; bodies of foreign nationals are held at the Institute of Legal Medicine in Havana until repatriation, where post-mortems are done the day of arrival. The funeral home provides the Spanish death certificate, the embalming certificate and burial licence, and a certificate permitting transfer of the remains. Mortuary storage is free for 3 days, then charged daily.
CU.authority: Cuban consulates (Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores, MINREX); Ministerio de Salud Publica

documents: Death certificate or death record from the country of death (for transcription at the Conservatória dos Registos Centrais; Portuguese translation if needed)
Transfer/removal authorisation (alvará) from the country of death, to be endorsed (visto) by the Cabo Verdean registrar
Medical certificate of cause of death / non-contagious disease (expected)
Embalming certificate (expected for air transport)
Passport or ID of the deceased (confirm with the registrar)
Burial request to the receiving municipal cemetery (Annex I form)
CV.coffin: A zinc coffin of at least 0.4 mm is mandatory for burial in a vault (jazigo), with gas filters and pressure devices; a wooden coffin suffices for a grave. When carried as normal freight by air or sea, the coffin must be placed in solid packaging that hides its appearance, marked 'manusear com precaução' (handle with care). Opening a zinc coffin is prohibited except on judicial order, for burial in a grave or for cremation.
CV.embalming: Not regulated by the decree for incoming bodies; embalming is expected by airlines and departure countries.
CV.consular: Decreto-Lei 15/2015 (art. 26): a body or ashes transferred from abroad need the transfer permit endorsed by the Conservador dos Registos Centrais in Praia, and the foreign death record is transcribed there; if the remains do not pass through Praia, the registrar of the area of entry endorses it. If the deceased was not Cabo Verdean, the diplomatic or consular representative of his or her country may apply. Cabo Verdean consulates do not publish a separate checklist. Not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
CV.arrival: Customs and health clearance at the international airport (Praia, Sal, Boa Vista or São Vicente); the coffin is carried by a hearse to the cemetery with a copy of the death certificate. Burial or cremation must take place within 72 hours of entry into Cabo Verde. Burial is requested from the municipal cemetery. Cremation is not available in practice.
CV.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights. A casket on a private aircraft should arrive at an international airport with customs and health officers, with the original documents. Plan the arrival island carefully: the transfer permit must be endorsed by the registrar and burial must follow within 72 hours of entry.
CV.export: The death must be registered at the Conservatória do Registo Civil, usually by the funeral director; certificates are only in Portuguese. No coffin may be sealed in zinc before 24 hours after death, nor before the death record or certificate is issued. Post mortems can take up to 10 days (only two pathologists). No legal timescale for repatriation; no cremation in Cabo Verde.
CV.authority: Conservatória dos Registos Centrais (Praia); municipal cemetery administration; Delegado de Saúde

documents: Medical statement from the competent doctor where the death occurred, or an extract of the death certificate (name, birth date/age, date and place of death, cause of death or statement that death was natural / not due to a contagious disease)
Statement from the person who embalmed or otherwise preserved the body, describing the method used
Statement from the competent authority of the place of death on how and by which route the body will be transported
CW.coffin: Hermetically sealed coffin made of impermeable material with absorbent material, containing only the body, its clothing, packing material and personal effects, packed to the satisfaction of the doctor designated by the Minister of Health, Environment and Nature in a well-closing outer coffin. The law does not name the material (zinc is not specified); confirm with the receiving funeral home. Name, first names, date of birth, date and place of death and destination must be clearly marked on the coffin. The law does not say who must witness the sealing at origin.
CW.embalming: Required: the body must be embalmed or properly preserved by another method. If the death was due to a quarantinable disease, arterial and cavity embalming is mandatory.
CW.consular: No consular step is set by the law; the transport statement must come from the competent authority of the country where the death occurred. Confirm with the receiving funeral home or the Curaçao civil registry whether legalisation, apostille or translation of foreign documents is needed.
CW.arrival: The three statements are presented on arrival. Bodies brought into Curaçao must be buried as soon as possible and only with written leave, issued free of charge, from the civil registrar (ambtenaar van de burgerlijke stand), which cannot be issued before the death statement is produced.
CW.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private aircraft. The same coffin and document rules apply as for cargo; confirm customs and health clearance arrangements for the arrival airport and arrange collection by a local funeral home.
CW.export: Leaving Curaçao: the same rules apply. The body must be embalmed or otherwise preserved, sealed in a hermetic impermeable coffin with absorbent material inside an outer coffin to the satisfaction of the doctor designated by the Minister of Health, Environment and Nature, labelled, and accompanied by the medical/death statement, the embalming statement and a transport statement for the authorities of the destination. Exhumed remains travel in a hermetically sealed coffin with the exhumation/transport permit where required and a death certificate extract. No typical delay is published.
CW.authority: Ministry of Health, Environment and Nature (GMN) and the Civil Registry (Burgerlijke Stand), Curaçao

documents: Laissez-passer for a corpse from the departure country (Strasbourg states) or its equivalent transport permit
Death certificate
Embalming certificate (where the departure country requires embalming)
Other documents as advised by the receiving Cypriot funeral director
CY.coffin: From Strasbourg states: hermetically sealed coffin with absorbent material, as required by the Agreement (in practice a zinc or other sealed metal liner inside a wooden coffin). Cyprus-specific rules for incoming coffins are not published online; confirm with the receiving Cypriot funeral director.
CY.embalming: Embalming is a legal requirement for repatriation from Cyprus. For incoming bodies follow the departure country's rules and confirm with the receiving funeral director; funerals in Cyprus are normally held within 24-48 hours of death.
CY.consular: From Strasbourg states the laissez-passer is sufficient. From other countries, ask the Cypriot embassy or consulate whether legalised documents are needed; Ministry of Health rules for incoming coffins are not published online.
CY.arrival: Customs and health clearance at the arrival airport; the receiving Cypriot funeral director arranges burial. There are no cremation facilities in Cyprus.
CY.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A sealed coffin is large and heavy, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at a Republic of Cyprus airport (Larnaca or Paphos): the Republic treats entry through the north, such as Ercan airport, as illegal entry.
CY.export: A local funeral director arranges repatriation: embalming is a legal requirement, and the funeral director provides the special casket and the documents, including a certificate of embalming. For Strasbourg destinations the laissez-passer is issued under the authority of the Director of Medical Services, Ministry of Health. Exhumation rules and typical delays are not published; confirm with the funeral director.
CY.authority: Ministry of Health, Department of Medical Services

documents: Laissez-passer for a corpse from the departure country (treaty states), or the Czech consulate's accompanying document (pruvodni list)
Foreign death certificate with apostille or consular legalisation, and an official translation if requested
Embalming certificate where required by the departure country
CZ.coffin: A sturdy coffin with a zinc liner meeting the international agreements (Strasbourg articles 6 and 7: watertight, absorbent material, only the body and personal effects).
CZ.embalming: Embalming is not usually mandatory in Czechia; follow the departure country's rules for incoming bodies. Bodies leaving Czechia normally travel with an embalming certificate.
CZ.consular: From non-treaty countries the Czech embassy or consulate must agree to the repatriation and issues the pruvodni list in paper form, sent to the funeral service by post (fee 200 CZK in local currency). The foreign death certificate needs an apostille or consular legalisation so it can be registered at the special registry office (zvlastni matrika) in Brno.
CZ.arrival: The coffin is cleared on arrival with its transport documents. The body must be handed to a licensed funeral service, which arranges burial or cremation; for a Czech citizen, the foreign death certificate is registered with the special registry office (zvlastni matrika).
CZ.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
CZ.export: For a foreigner who dies in Czechia, the regional public health station (krajska hygienicka stanice) issues the pruvodni list (laissez-passer) required under the applicable agreement. For a destination outside the agreements, that state's embassy or consulate must consent, based on proof of death and confirmation of no criminal or health objection. On request and at the applicant's cost, customs can seal the coffin at the funeral home, crematorium or public health station and record the seal on the transport documents. The body is normally embalmed and travels in a zinc-lined coffin. Funerals must be ordered within 96 hours, though authorities normally allow more time for foreigners.
CZ.authority: Regional public health stations (Ministry of Health); Czech embassies and consulates (Ministry of Foreign Affairs)

documents: Laissez-passer for a corpse (Leichenpass) issued by the departure country's authority
Death certificate (an international multilingual version can avoid translation)
Medical certificate of cause of death
Embalming certificate where required by the departure country
DE.coffin: Under the Berlin agreement: a hermetically closed (soldered) metal coffin, with absorbent material in the bottom, placed inside a wooden coffin at least 3 cm thick with watertight joints. Zinc is the usual metal; confirm any state-specific rules with the receiving funeral director.
DE.embalming: No federal embalming rule for incoming bodies is published; follow the departure country's rules and confirm with the receiving German funeral director.
DE.consular: German embassies and consulates can help with contacts to local authorities abroad. Whether foreign documents need legalisation, an apostille or a translation depends on the country of death; ask the German mission or the receiving funeral director.
DE.arrival: Customs clearance at the arrival airport; the receiving German funeral director arranges burial or cremation. Burial and cremation rules differ between the federal states.
DE.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
DE.export: The Leichenpass is issued by the local authority of the place of death (e.g. the public order office in Stuttgart, EUR 70), on application by the funeral company, with the medical death certificate, the civil death certificate and all documents required for a burial. If there are signs of an unnatural death or the person is unidentified, approval by the public prosecutor or a judge is required first. Under the Berlin agreement the body travels in a soldered metal coffin inside a wooden coffin; the rules of the destination and transit countries also apply.
DE.authority: Local authorities of the federal states (Leichenpass); German missions abroad

documents: Ligpas (laissez-passer for a corpse) from the sending state's competent authority
Death certificate (translation may be requested)
Embalming certificate where required by the sending state
DK.coffin: Moisture-proof coffin with absorbent material: either an outer wooden coffin with sides at least 20 mm thick and a carefully soldered zinc inner coffin, or a single wooden coffin at least 30 mm thick lined with zinc. For air transport a pressure-equalising device with filter is required unless the coffin has a soldered zinc inner coffin and the body is embalmed. Transfers to and from Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden only need a tight, solid coffin.
DK.embalming: Not required as such. For air transport, a coffin with a soldered zinc inner coffin needs either an embalming certificate or a certificate for an approved pressure-equalising device with filter; a single zinc-lined wooden coffin always needs the device. For incoming bodies the sending state's rules also apply.
DK.consular: No Danish consular step is set by the regulation: the sending state's ligpas is the key document. The Danish embassy or consulate can advise on bringing a coffin or urn home; ask it whether the foreign death certificate needs legalisation or translation.
DK.arrival: The death is reported to the parish (church) office, which also serves as the burial request; the receiving Danish undertaker arranges this. Burial or cremation generally takes place within eight days of death.
DK.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside. The Danish coffin rules for air transport (zinc inner coffin plus embalming, or an approved pressure valve) apply to any aircraft.
DK.export: The ligpas for a body leaving Denmark is issued by the Danish Patient Safety Authority (Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed, which took over the former embedslaege role). The request form records the route and transport mode and the undertaker's attestation that the coffin meets Executive Order 152/1983 and holds only the body and permitted personal effects, with a soldering certificate for a zinc inner coffin and, for air transport, an embalming certificate or a pressure-equalising device certificate. Transport must start as soon as possible and no later than 8 days after death unless the issuing authority grants an extension.
DK.authority: Danish Patient Safety Authority (Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed) for the ligpas; parish offices for burial

documents: Original death certificate issued by the vital records office of the place of death
Certificate of no contagious disease (certificacion de no contagio) from the local health department
Embalming certificate signed by the funeral director or embalmer, notarised
Removal or transit permit where the country of departure issues one (confirm with the consulate)
DO.coffin: Not specified on the consulate page. A hermetically sealed coffin is the usual international standard for air transport; confirm with the Dominican consulate and the airline.
DO.embalming: Required in practice: the consulate's list for a body includes a notarised embalming certificate. The UK government also lists an embalming certificate among documents for repatriation out of the Dominican Republic.
DO.consular: Documents are submitted to the Dominican consulate covering the place of death (the New York consulate publishes the checklist; tel. +1 212 768 2480, infony@mirex.gob.do). For cremated remains the death and cremation certificates must be apostilled by the US Department of State. Holders of a valid Dominican electronic ordinary passport are covered by a free repatriation insurance with Seguros Reservas (up to USD 9,000; notify Seguros Reservas within 48 hours of the death; 6-month waiting period for death from illness), per the Direccion General de Pasaportes.
DO.arrival: Not published officially. The receiving Dominican funeral home normally handles customs and health clearance at the airport. Confirm burial or cremation formalities with the funeral home.
DO.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an international airport with customs and health officers (for example Santo Domingo Las Americas or Punta Cana) and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. No specific rule for private flights carrying remains was found.
DO.export: To send a body out of the Dominican Republic, the death is registered at the Civil Registry office nearest to where it occurred; the death certificate is usually issued within 3 working days. All foreign nationals who die in the country undergo a post-mortem at the Pathology Institute in Santo Domingo or Santiago. The UK government lists the documents for repatriation as the civil registry death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains. Dominican death certificates are in Spanish and do not state the cause of death; check whether the destination requires it.
DO.authority: Dominican consulate in the country of departure (Ministry of Foreign Affairs, MIREX); Civil Registry and Pathology Institute (exit)

documents: Death certificate
Medical certificate that the body is free from infection
Embalming certificate from the funeral services
Undertaker's certificate that the coffin contains only the named deceased
Certificate that the body was prepared according to Muslim rites
Export or release permit from the country of death (for example a coroner's out of England certificate)
Identity documents of the deceased, including the consular card; birth certificate if not registered at the consulate
DZ.coffin: Under Decree 16-77 (art. 12) a hermetic coffin, built to specifications set by joint order of the Interior and Health ministers, is compulsory when transport exceeds 100 km and more than 24 hours pass between coffining and burial, when death was due to a contagious disease, or when the wali so decides. A coffin flown from abroad therefore needs to be hermetically sealed; confirm the liner type (usually zinc) with the consulate and the funeral home.
DZ.embalming: Algerian consulates list an embalming certificate among the required documents, together with a certificate of Muslim ritual washing. Ask the consulate if a non-embalmed body is acceptable.
DZ.consular: The Algerian consulate issues the transfer authorisation and the Algerian death certificate, and informs the family and Algerian authorities of the arrival date. The funeral services appointed by the family usually file the paperwork.
DZ.arrival: The coffin is cleared at the arrival airport and released to the family or a funeral service. The president of the communal people's assembly (APC) of the burial place issues the burial authorisation. Muslim burial takes place as soon as possible.
DZ.private_aviation: No rule specific to remains on private aircraft was found. The consular transfer authorisation must travel with the coffin, and the handling agent must arrange clearance at the arrival airport.
DZ.export: Leaving Algeria: the death is registered at the town hall (certificate usually in Arabic or French, no cause of death). For a foreign national, transport of the body to the home country is authorised by the wali of the place of death, and the Minister of the Interior is informed (Decree 16-77, art. 10). For British nationals, the British Embassy issues a mortuary pass and power of attorney; other nationals should ask their embassy. Autopsies, when ordered, are usually done within 24 hours. If repatriation does not happen within 15 days, local authorities proceed with burial; the public prosecutor can approve one extension.
DZ.authority: Algerian embassies and consulates; Ministry of the Interior and walis for exits

documents: Death certificate or equivalent from the country of death, apostilled or legalised, in the original language with Spanish translation
Embalming certificate (or cremation certificate for ashes)
Transfer permit from the competent authority of the country of death showing name, surname, age, place and cause of death
Certified copy of the forensic autopsy report, legalised or apostilled, for violent deaths
Identity card or passport of the relative or applicant (relative up to 4th degree of consanguinity or 2nd of affinity)
If no relatives: sworn statement, or written authorisation of relatives to a third party with ID copies
EC.coffin: Regulation 000001-2022 (art. 27) requires entry and exit of bodies to comply with the IATA cargo manual conditions; art. 34 says the coffin must meet the regulation's technical characteristics. The regulation does not name a material; confirm the coffin type (usually hermetically sealed, metal-lined, in an outer case) with the airline and the receiving funeral home. No official witness of sealing is required by the text.
EC.embalming: Required for entry: an embalming certificate (or cremation certificate) is a mandatory document (art. 34). The preservation certificate must state why it was done, identification data, the technique and the substances and materials used (art. 23). Embalming is prohibited for the infectious-disease cases listed in Annex 1 of the regulation (art. 19).
EC.consular: No consular transfer permit is listed for entry; the death certificate must be apostilled (Ecuador is a Hague Apostille party) or legalised and translated into Spanish. If no relatives are present, a special power of attorney or a diplomatic note from the consular representative authorising final disposal is accepted (art. 29). Ecuador is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
EC.arrival: The Ministry of Public Health office at the point of entry checks the documents and issues the authorisation form, free of charge. Offices: Quito Mariscal Sucre airport (Mon-Fri 07:00-22:30), Guayaquil Jose Joaquin de Olmedo airport (24 h daily), and the Rumichaca, Huaquillas and Macara land borders. Documents can be sent in advance by email. A local funeral home then collects the coffin.
EC.private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights. Arrive at Quito or Guayaquil, where the Ministry of Public Health has an office issuing the entry authorisation; note Quito's office is open Mon-Fri 07:00-22:30 only, while Guayaquil is open 24 hours. Send the documents by email beforehand.
EC.export: Exit needs a Ministry of Public Health sanitary authorisation issued at the point of exit (art. 35), free of charge, on presentation of: a legalised copy of the Registro Civil death record (or an authorisation certified by the destination country's consul in Ecuador), the embalming or cremation certificate, the autopsy report if any, and the applicant's ID. The destination country's rules must also be met (art. 36). Medical death certificate on the INEC form, post-mortem for sudden, violent or unexplained deaths; cremation not allowed after violent deaths.
EC.authority: Ministry of Public Health (Ministerio de Salud Publica), offices at international points of entry; Regulation 000001-2022

documents: Laissez-passer for a corpse from the departure country (Strasbourg states) or its equivalent transport permit
Death certificate
Embalming certificate where required by the departure country
Funeral director's sealing certificate
EE.coffin: Hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin filled with a desiccant, placed in a tightly closed wooden box (Cemeteries Act section 3(2)). If death was caused by an extremely dangerous, highly infectious disease (yellow fever, viral haemorrhagic fever, smallpox, plague or anthrax), the body must first be wrapped in an antiseptic-impregnated shroud.
EE.embalming: No Estonian embalming requirement found; follow the departure country's rules. The Cemeteries Act sets no fixed burial deadline but requires burial or cremation without undue delay.
EE.consular: Estonia's declared competent authorities under the Strasbourg Agreement are the Ministry of Social Affairs and Estonian diplomatic missions. From non-party countries, ask the Estonian embassy what documents or legalisation are required.
EE.arrival: Customs clearance at the arrival airport; the receiving Estonian funeral director arranges burial with the cemetery or cremation.
EE.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
EE.export: Bodies leaving Estonia must be in a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin with desiccant, in a tightly closed wooden box (Cemeteries Act). A local funeral director must be instructed and works with international undertakers. A post-mortem is normally performed, always when death was not natural, and repatriation can go ahead once the authorities are content that no further examinations are needed. The death must be registered within 7 days. The authority issuing the laissez-passer is not published in English; the funeral director arranges it.
EE.authority: Ministry of Social Affairs; Estonian diplomatic missions

documents: Original death certificate, certified and translated into Arabic by the Egyptian mission
Egyptian passport of the deceased (stamped cancelled) or Egyptian national ID card
Certificate from the health authorities of the country of death that death was not caused by a contagious epidemic disease
Permit from the authorities of the country of death to transport and bury the body
Funeral home certificate that the body was prepared, embalmed and cased under international health rules
Egyptian consular permit to transport the body to Egypt
EG.coffin: The funeral home must place the body in a casket meeting international health rules; Egyptian missions do not publish a specific casket specification. Confirm the casket type (usually hermetically sealed, metal-lined, in an outer case) with the consulate and the airline.
EG.embalming: The Egyptian mission asks for a funeral home certificate that the body was embalmed or prepared for travel. Embalming is also required for bodies leaving Egypt.
EG.consular: The Egyptian embassy or consulate reviews the originals, certifies and translates the death certificate (the Washington embassy lists fees of USD 47 for certification and USD 52 for translation) and issues the transport permit. Mailed certification and translation files are returned within about 10 working days; no timeframe is published for the transport permit.
EG.arrival: The coffin is cleared at the arrival airport and released to the family or a funeral service. Burial usually follows quickly; confirm local formalities with the receiving funeral service.
EG.private_aviation: No rule specific to remains on private aircraft was found. Land at an airport with customs and health services and have the handling agent arrange clearance of the coffin.
EG.export: Leaving Egypt: the death is registered at the district health office and an Arabic death certificate is issued. Embalming is needed for repatriation. The local undertaker needs a permission letter signed and stamped by the deceased's embassy (as the British Embassy issues for UK nationals). Postmortems are carried out by the Egyptian authorities without next-of-kin consent; if the forensic report is not final, the certificate may say the cause is not yet determined, which still allows repatriation.
EG.authority: Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (embassies and consulates)

documents: Two certified copies of the death certificate
Non-contagious disease letter from a state, county or municipal health official
Non-contagious disease letter from the attending physician
Funeral home preparation letter (procedures, casket contents, consignee name, address and phone)
Copies of the deceased's Eritrean passport or ID card, plus foreign passport or residence permit
ER.coffin: The consulates prefer a steel casket inside a wooden outer shipping container. A wooden casket is accepted with a steel screw-down liner for sealing and a wooden outer box.
ER.embalming: Not specified by the consulates. The preparation letter must describe how the body was prepared, and embalming is the usual practice.
ER.consular: The consulates (e.g. Washington and Frankfurt) require Eritrean nationality, shown by an Eritrean passport or national ID or other proof. Documents are submitted by email. Fees and processing time are not published. Eritrea is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
ER.arrival: Not officially published. Plan collection at Asmara by the family or a local funeral service.
ER.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A private aircraft carrying a casket must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services; have the local handling agent and receiving funeral home confirm in advance that the remains can be cleared from a private flight. Eritrea has strict entry and permit controls; obtain all authorisations before departure.
ER.export: To take a body out of Eritrea you need a death certificate issued by the Zoba (regional) Administration, the hospital death certificate form or dead body certificate, the passport of the deceased, a police clearance letter, an airport immigration police approval letter and an embalming certificate. The Zoba Administration also provides an English translation of the death certificate.
ER.authority: Eritrean embassy or consulate; Zoba Administration and police (exit)

documents: Salvoconducto mortuorio (laissez-passer) from a Strasbourg or Berlin agreement state, OR Documento Unico from the Spanish consulate
Consular route: medical cause-of-death certificate, embalming or temporary conservation certificate, civil registry death certificate, judicial permit if the death was violent
Sanidad Exterior entry authorisation obtained through SISAEX by the funeral company
ES.coffin: A coffin suitable for international transport, hermetically sealed; the US Embassy notes a certificate of placement in a sealed coffin is issued for shipments. Simplified bilateral rules with France and Portugal apply to land transport only.
ES.embalming: Bodies via the consular route need an embalming or temporary conservation certificate, and bodies leaving Spain must be embalmed or temporarily conserved. Embalming must be done 24-48 hours after death under medical supervision; embalmed bodies must be buried within 96 hours. A person who died of a contagious disease cannot be embalmed.
ES.consular: From countries outside the Strasbourg and Berlin agreements, the family applies to the Spanish consulate in the country of death, which reviews the documents and issues a Documento Unico to be presented to Sanidad Exterior on arrival. From agreement countries no consular step is needed.
ES.arrival: The funeral company requests entry through SISAEX to the Sanidad Exterior service at the entry point; once approved, the authorisation is downloaded and presented to customs for release. The receiving funeral director handles burial or cremation under regional mortuary health rules.
ES.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A sealed international coffin is long and heavy, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside. The Sanidad Exterior authorisation names the entry point, so the private flight must land at the airport declared in the SISAEX request.
ES.export: The funeral company files the exit request via SISAEX with Sanidad Exterior in the province of death or of exit. The body must be embalmed or temporarily conserved and placed in a coffin suitable for international transport. For Strasbourg/Berlin destinations Sanidad Exterior issues the salvoconducto mortuorio; other destinations need their consulate's entry authorisation first. The US Embassy estimates 9-10 working days for an overseas shipment.
ES.authority: Ministry of Health, Sanidad Exterior (via SISAEX)

documents: Death certificate (original and copy)
Funeral home letter confirming embalming and a hermetically sealed casket (original and copy)
Non-contagious disease letter from the local health authority (original and copy)
Burial permit (original and copy)
Copy of the deceased's passport; if not an Ethiopian passport holder, a letter from the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs permitting entry
ET.coffin: A hermetically sealed casket is required, confirmed in the funeral home letter.
ET.embalming: Required: the funeral home must confirm the body was embalmed or preserved by standard methods.
ET.consular: The embassy reviews the file and issues a permit for shipping the body, free of charge. The Washington embassy says it issues the permit quickly once the file is complete, and emails it to be printed in colour. Applications are rejected without a passport showing Ethiopia as place of birth, or without the Ministry of Foreign Affairs letter for non-passport holders. Ethiopia is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
ET.arrival: The embassy says the transport rules for human remains are set by Ethiopian Airlines. Arrival is at Addis Ababa Bole, where the family or a funeral home collects the casket.
ET.private_aviation: The embassy defers to Ethiopian Airlines for the transport rules. For a private flight, confirm with the Bole handling agent and the Ethiopian Civil Aviation Authority how remains are cleared. No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A private aircraft carrying a casket must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services; have the local handling agent and receiving funeral home confirm in advance that the remains can be cleared from a private flight.
ET.export: For a death in Ethiopia, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issues a letter permitting repatriation (sometimes called a No Objection letter). It is issued after it receives a Letter of Release from the deceased's embassy, the local death certificate and any autopsy report. Most airlines require an autopsy before repatriation. Local undertakers can supply international caskets. Formalities normally take a week or more.
ET.authority: Ethiopian embassy or consulate; Ministry of Foreign Affairs (exit)

documents: Laissez-passer for a corpse from the departure state (Strasbourg countries), or the removal permit and documents required by the country of death
Foreign death certificate (legalisation or translation may be needed; a funeral home can arrange it)
Cause-of-death investigation documents, which travel with the coffin for the Finnish police
Embalming certificate and certificate of non-contagious death where the departure country or airline requires them
FI.coffin: Strasbourg standard, reproduced on Finnish municipal laissez-passer forms: impermeable coffin with absorbent material, either an outer wooden coffin (sides at least 20 mm) with an inner soldered coffin of zinc or other self-destroying material, or a wooden coffin of at least 30 mm lined with zinc or other self-destroying material; for air transport, a purifying (pressure-equalising) device or guarantees of strength accepted by the departure authority. Finland's rule for coffins from non-Strasbourg countries is not published; the departure country's rules apply.
FI.embalming: No Finnish entry requirement is published. The departure country's rules and the airline's requirements apply.
FI.consular: No Finnish consular permit is needed for entry. The Finnish embassy or consulate in the country of death advises on burial, cremation and transport, and can receive notice of the death for a Finnish citizen. The death must also be notified to the Digital and Population Data Services Agency with the original foreign death certificate (which may need legalisation or translation).
FI.arrival: When a coffin or urn is brought to Finland, contact the police of the deceased's last home municipality, or of the municipality of burial. The cause-of-death documents are handed to that police department, which may order an additional investigation in Finland if the foreign one is inadequate and establishes identity. No separate burial permit is required. The receiving Finnish funeral home collects the coffin.
FI.private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights; the coffin needs the same documents as airline cargo. Finland is in the Schengen area: a flight from outside Schengen must land at an airport with border and customs control. A sealed international coffin is long and heavy, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket.
FI.export: The hospital or doctor issues the Finnish death certificate; if the death is unexpected, the police may order a forensic autopsy (the final cause-of-death certificate can take 4-6 months). Under Decree 226/1989 (amended 849/1993), the laissez-passer for a corpse (ruumiinkuljetuslupa) is issued by the health inspector designated by the municipal body of the municipality where the international transport begins (municipal environmental health services). It certifies the Strasbourg coffin standard and states the cause of death in English or French, by WHO code, or in a sealed envelope. A Finnish funeral director arranges the coffin and transport; confirm embalming needs with the destination country and airline.
FI.authority: Police of the home or burial municipality (entry); municipal health inspector (laissez-passer for exit); Digital and Population Data Services Agency (registration)

documents: Application letter to the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Health and Medical Services
Death certificate or medical cause of death certificate
Doctor's letter that the death was not from an infectious disease and the remains are not infectious
Embalming certificate stating how the body was embalmed
Funeral home sealing certificate that the casket is hygienically sealed for transport
Passport bio page of the deceased and of the consignee; flight itinerary
English or certified English translation; originals presented on arrival
FJ.coffin: The funeral home must issue a sealing certificate stating that the casket is hygienically sealed and safe for air or sea transport. No further casket specification (such as zinc lining) is published; confirm with the airline.
FJ.embalming: Required: an embalming certificate stating how the remains were embalmed must accompany the application.
FJ.consular: No consular permit is required, but documents must be in English or certified translation. Fiji embassies can write a supporting letter to help expedite the repatriation.
FJ.arrival: The Nadi Airport Health Office carries out the clearance on arrival, and original documents must be presented. Fee FJD 172.50 on arrival; FJD 230 if the remains arrive without prior notification; FJD 345 if infectious remains need health supervision. Contact Air Terminal Services (Fiji) in advance to ensure space and staff to handle the remains; a local funeral home collects.
FJ.private_aviation: The published procedure applies to all flights and vessels and is handled through the Nadi Airport Health Office. For a private flight, send the documents in advance and arrange arrival at Nadi with customs, quarantine and the airport health officer present.
FJ.export: The same Ministry of Health procedure applies to remains leaving Fiji: application letter to the Permanent Secretary, death certificate, non-infectious disease letter, embalming certificate, funeral home sealing certificate, passports and itinerary, emailed in advance to the Nadi Airport Health Office. Departure fee FJD 115. Processing about 24 to 48 hours, longer at weekends and public holidays.
FJ.authority: Ministry of Health and Medical Services (Nadi Airport Health Office)

documents: Form COR25B, Notification to HM Coroner of intended repatriation to the Falkland Islands
Certificate of Death or a Coroner's Interim Certificate of the Fact of Death
Copy of the deceased's passport
Certificate for burial or cremation
Consent of the next of kin (if the applicant is not the next of kin)
Other documents issued about the death, such as inquest notes, freedom from infection certificate and embalming certificate
FK.coffin: Not specified by Falklands rules. Use a sealed coffin that meets the requirements of the airline or the South Atlantic Airbridge and of the countries of transit; confirm with the carrier.
FK.embalming: Not stated as mandatory; the Coroner asks for any embalming certificate issued. Confirm embalming needs with the carrier and the transit countries.
FK.consular: Not applicable: the Falklands are a British Overseas Territory with no consulates of their own. The UK is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. HM Coroner (Courts and Tribunals Department, Stanley) is the point of contact.
FK.arrival: HM Coroner must be notified of every incoming repatriation, with the details on form COR25B; the form need not be filed before travel, but the information is required on arrival and delays in providing it may delay release or burial. A local undertaker receives the coffin; confirm customs clearance with the undertaker. Deaths are registered at the Registry in Stanley.
FK.private_aviation: Any aircraft landing in the Falklands needs a Foreign Carrier Permit from the Falkland Islands Civil Aviation Department (FICAD); charters use a Short Term permit (up to 14 days) and private flights a Letter of Permission carried on board. Apply at least 14 days before the flight (medical flights excepted). Prior permission is required to land at Stanley (SFAL) or Mount Pleasant (EGYP). UK-registered aircraft need no permit but must notify FICAD. Usual routes for remains are the South Atlantic Airbridge from RAF Brize Norton or LATAM via South America.
FK.export: No permission from HM Coroner is needed to take a body out, but by local practice the Coroner confirms no objection; file form COR25 with the Coroner's office. For the South Atlantic Airbridge you need: who is financially responsible, confirmation an undertaker will meet the flight at RAF Brize Norton, Customs confirmation, a Certificate of Death or Interim Certificate of Fact of Death, a Coroner's Order for Removal of Body from Jurisdiction, a certificate of personal particulars, a Free From Infection Certificate from King Edward VII Memorial Hospital, an Order for Burial/Cremation if applicable, and the passport. Deaths are registered at the Registry in Stanley (within 5 days in Stanley, 14 elsewhere).
FK.authority: HM Coroner, Courts and Tribunals Department, Falkland Islands Government; Falkland Islands Civil Aviation Department; Registry Services

documents: Certified death certificate (original)
Certified burial transit permit (original)
Certified letter of non-contagious disease (original)
Embalmer's affidavit and report
Copy of the deceased's passport, birth certificate, ID or driver's licence
Bill of lading (air waybill)
Travel itinerary
FM.coffin: No FSM-specific casket standard is published: the Embassy states that funeral homes must comply with the airline's casket and shipping requirements and should consult the carrier.
FM.embalming: Embalming is expected: the Embassy's checklist requires an embalmer's affidavit and report for a body. Cremated remains need only the death certificate, cremation certificate and an ID copy.
FM.consular: The FSM Embassy in Washington and the Consulates General (Honolulu, Guam) coordinate the request with the FSM authorities receiving the remains. The Embassy says travel authorization documents for remains are no longer required. No consular fee or legalisation requirement is published. The FSM Government does not pay repatriation costs.
FM.arrival: Arrival is at the airport of the receiving state (Pohnpei, Chuuk, Yap or Kosrae), with the original documents enclosed with the remains. Pohnpei State has its own application for the importation of human remains; confirm local clearance with the receiving state's health department. The family or its designee collects. No legal burial deadline was found in national law; the Director of Health Services may regulate interments and dead bodies (41 FSMC 102).
FM.private_aviation: No rule specific to human remains on private flights was found. A private aircraft needs FSM landing clearance and the usual border formalities at the state airport; the casket must still travel with the original documents listed by the Embassy.
FM.export: No published national export procedure was found. Confirm the required certificates and health clearance with the state health department, and the entry rules of the destination country (for the US, CDC import rules).
FM.authority: FSM Department of Health and Social Affairs and state health departments; FSM Embassy (Washington) and Consulates

documents: Local death certificate (transcription into the French civil register by the consulate is recommended)
Authorisation to transport the body issued by the French embassy or consulate (or the laissez-passer for the corpse when the death occurred in another Strasbourg Agreement country)
Medical certificate stating the death was not from a contagious disease, where the departure country requires it
Embalming certificate where required by the departure country
Burial or cremation arrangements in France (receiving funeral director)
FR.coffin: For air transport an airtight coffin (cercueil hermétique, a metal box) is mandatory. Confirm with the receiving French funeral director in advance if cremation is planned after arrival.
FR.embalming: No French rule specific to incoming bodies is published on the official pages; embalming depends on the departure country and the airline.
FR.consular: The French embassy or consulate (with the Crisis and Support Centre where relevant) issues the authorisation to transport the body or ashes to France, and can transcribe the local death certificate into French civil status. It can give an indicative cost and contacts for local and French funeral directors. Families bear all costs. France has been a party to the Strasbourg Agreement since 10 June 2000.
FR.arrival: The receiving French funeral director takes charge at the airport. Burial or cremation must take place no later than the 14th calendar day after the body enters France (CGCT art. R2213-33, decree 2024-790). The prefect may grant exceptions; a local derogation cannot go beyond the 21st calendar day.
FR.private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. An airtight metal-lined coffin is long and heavy, so it must fit through the cargo door and into the cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. France requires an airtight coffin for any air transport, including private flights. A flight from outside the Schengen area must land at an airport with border and customs control.
FR.export: To send a coffin out of France, the funeral company obtains authorisation from the prefect of the place where the coffin is closed. The same rule applies to EU and non-EU destinations. An airtight (metal-lined) coffin is mandatory for air transport. Ashes need authorisation from the prefect of the place of cremation or of the applicant's residence. The destination country's consular requirements also apply. The death is registered at the town hall (mairie), which issues the death certificate.
FR.authority: French embassy or consulate abroad (entry); prefect of the department (exit)

documents: Foreign death certificate with certified English translation
Permission to remove the body issued by a coroner or equivalent authority abroad
Embalming and non-contagious disease certificates where issued by the departure country
Passport of the deceased
For cremation in England and Wales: coroner's certificate (form Cremation 6)
For Scotland: DCRS Form Y (request for repatriation) with supporting documents
GB.coffin: UK law sets no specific import coffin standard. The coffin must meet the requirements of the airline and of the country of departure; confirm with the funeral directors.
GB.embalming: Not required by UK law for import; the departure country or airline may require it. Tell the funeral director if a UK inquest is likely.
GB.consular: No UK consular legalisation or entry permit is needed. British embassies can give lists of funeral directors but cannot pay costs. The UK is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
GB.arrival: The UK funeral director collects the coffin. In England and Wales, take the foreign death certificate to the register office for the area of the funeral to get a certificate of no liability to register. Tell the coroner if the death was violent, unnatural or of unknown cause, as an inquest is likely. In Scotland, the body cannot be buried or cremated until DCRS has authorised it; DCRS aims to do this within 5 working days. Northern Ireland has its own process.
GB.private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. A sealed international coffin is long and heavy, so it must fit through the cargo door and into the cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. For international general aviation flights, a General Aviation Report must be submitted online in advance through an approved method (penalty up to GBP 10,000). Arrive at an airport able to provide customs clearance and declare the remains.
GB.export: To take a body out of England, the funeral director gives notice (Form 104) to the coroner for the area where the body lies, using the death certificate, the deceased's passport and the applicant's passport. The coroner issues the Out of England form (Form 103), usually within 4 working days when the death is not being investigated, longer after a post-mortem. Do not book travel until the funeral director has Form 103. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own procedures.
GB.authority: Register office and coroner (England and Wales); Death Certification Review Service (Scotland); HM Revenue and Customs at entry

documents: Official certificate of the cause of death from the registrar of deaths or similar authority
Statement by the person who prepared the remains, certified by an appropriate authority, describing the preparation and confirming the coffin holds only the body and clothing
Transit permit stating name, age and sex (or a permit also naming cause of death, embalmer, coroner and public health officer)
GD.coffin: Impervious coffin: a container hermetically sealed by gasket or by soldered/welded metal, or a plastic container sealed by heat or adhesive. No official witnessing of the sealing is described.
GD.embalming: Proper embalming, or thorough washing and disinfection with packing and a disinfectant-soaked sheet, before shipment.
GD.consular: No legalisation step is set out in the regulations. Ask the Grenada mission in the country of death whether documents must be authenticated.
GD.arrival: The documents must accompany the shipment. Customs and health clearance at the port of entry; the local funeral home collects. No legal burial deadline was found.
GD.pouch: The regulations allow a properly embalmed body in an air disaster bag or in a plastic container sealed by heat or adhesive; confirm with the airline what outer packaging it requires.
GD.private_aviation: No private-flight rules found. Land at an airport of entry with customs and health officers and keep the documents with the remains.
GD.export: Leaving Grenada: the death certificate (English, with cause of death) is issued by the Registrar General's Department, usually within a few days. Post-mortems usually take place 2-3 days after the body reaches the mortuary. The local funeral director provides the certificate of embalming and permission to transfer the remains. One crematorium operates on the island.
GD.authority: Ministry of Health (port health) and Customs, under the Human Remains (Importation Control) Regulations

documents: Local death certificate (transcription into French civil status recommended)
Medical certificate of cause of death or non-contagious disease (usually asked)
Embalming or conservation certificate where the departure country requires it
Body transport authorisation issued by the French embassy or consulate
Burial or cremation arrangements in French Guiana (receiving funeral director)
GF.coffin: An airtight coffin (cercueil hermétique, a metal box) is mandatory for air transport under French rules. Confirm with the receiving funeral director in advance if cremation is planned.
GF.embalming: No French rule specific to incoming bodies is published on the official pages; embalming depends on the departure country and the airline. Confirm with the consulate.
GF.consular: The French embassy or consulate in the country of death issues the authorisation to transport the body or ashes and can transcribe the foreign death certificate. Families pay all costs. France is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement; whether its laissez-passer is used for French Guiana was not confirmed, and none of the neighbouring South American countries is a party.
GF.arrival: The receiving funeral director takes charge of the coffin at the airport. Burial or cremation must take place no later than the 14th calendar day after the body arrives in the overseas department (CGCT art. R2213-33, decree 2024-790). The prefect may grant exceptions; a local derogation cannot go beyond the 21st calendar day.
GF.private_aviation: The French airtight-coffin rule applies to any air transport, including private flights. Land at Cayenne Felix Eboue (the international airport with customs) and arrange for the receiving funeral director to meet the aircraft. The documents travel with the coffin.
GF.export: A funeral director handles the procedure. Transport of a body out of French Guiana, abroad or to mainland France, is authorised by the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed (Prefecture of French Guiana). An airtight coffin is mandatory by air. Ashes need authorisation from the prefect of the place of cremation or of the applicant's residence. The destination country's consular rules also apply.
GF.authority: French embassy or consulate abroad (entry); Prefect of French Guiana (exit)

documents: Certified copy of the death certificate
Burial and/or transit permit issued in the country of death
Embalmer's (non-contagious) affidavit or embalming certificate
Non-contagious disease letter or free-from-infection certificate from the local health authority
Copy of the deceased's passport or other Ghanaian identification
GH.coffin: A hermetically sealed casket in an all-wood outer shipping container (Ghana Embassy, Washington).
GH.embalming: Required: the Washington embassy lists embalming by the US standard method; the London High Commission asks for an embalming certificate.
GH.consular: The Washington embassy authenticates the file for USD 50, with documents in triplicate (original plus two copies). In London, a valid Ghanaian passport normally means no further High Commission document is needed; otherwise the High Commission issues a letter that serves as the travel document (fee GBP 30), on a certified death certificate, embalming certificate, free-from-infection certificate, Ghanaian ID of the deceased (or of a relative with a letter confirming identity and relationship) and two passport photos. Ghana is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
GH.arrival: Not officially detailed. The family or a Ghanaian funeral home collects the casket at Accra Kotoka. Cremated remains need the death certificate, cremation certificate and a hermetically sealed container.
GH.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A private aircraft carrying a casket must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services; have the local handling agent and receiving funeral home confirm in advance that the remains can be cleared from a private flight.
GH.export: The death is registered at the local births and deaths registry, usually by the funeral director. The hospital issues the cause-of-death certificate, usually within a week. An export licence is needed, which the funeral director obtains. For transfer to the UK, the body must be embalmed and placed in a zinc-lined coffin. A post-mortem is performed when the death is unknown, unnatural, sudden or violent.
GH.authority: Ghana embassy or High Commission; Ghana registry and funeral director (exit)

documents: Death certificate from the country of origin
Embalming certificate
Repatriation (removal) permit from the country of origin
From England or Wales: the coroner's acknowledgement of the Form 104 notice of removal
GI.coffin: Hermetically sealed coffin, often zinc-lined, meeting transport standards (Environmental Agency Gibraltar).
GI.embalming: Required for remains entering and leaving Gibraltar (Environmental Agency Gibraltar).
GI.consular: No Gibraltar consular permit is described. Gibraltar is not covered by the Strasbourg Agreement (the UK is not a party). The departure country issues the repatriation permit.
GI.arrival: The Environmental Agency and HM Customs Gibraltar must be notified in advance; airlines accept remains only with the correct paperwork. A Gibraltar funeral director usually liaises with the airline, consulates and local authorities and collects the coffin.
GI.private_aviation: All non-scheduled flights into Gibraltar airport need a Prior Permission Request accepted by the handling agent (GibAir, handling@gibair.gi). Third-country commercial operators also need Gibraltar Civil Aviation Authority permission and a Foreign Operator Permit (fees from 1 September 2026). A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket.
GI.export: The same rules apply when leaving: embalming, hermetically sealed coffin, Gibraltar death certificate (Civil Status and Registration Office), embalming certificate and a repatriation permit; notify the Environmental Agency and HM Customs in advance. Extra documents may be requested for infectious disease. The Coroner is involved where a death is reported to him. Destination countries apply their own consular rules.
GI.authority: Environmental Agency Gibraltar; HM Customs Gibraltar; Civil Status and Registration Office; Coroner of Gibraltar

documents: From Denmark: ligpas issued by the Danish Patient Safety Authority's medical officer service (in Copenhagen, the Stadslægen), on the request form for transport abroad including Greenland
Soldering certificate for the zinc coffin
Embalming certificate or certificate for an approved pressure-equalising device with filter (air transport)
Death certificate (Danish death certificate extract)
GL.coffin: Under Danish order no. 152 of 14 April 1983 (sections 2-3), as stated on the Patient Safety Authority's request form for transport abroad including Greenland: an outer wooden coffin (sides at least 20 mm) with an inner carefully soldered zinc coffin (soldering certificate attached), or a single wooden coffin with sides of at least 30 mm lined with zinc. The carrier may set additional requirements; confirm with the airline.
GL.embalming: For air transport from Denmark: embalming certificate or an approved pressure-equalising device with filter (required with the double coffin; the device is required with the zinc-lined single coffin).
GL.consular: No consular step from Denmark. From other countries, Danish embassies represent Greenland; no specific Greenland entry permit was found. Denmark is not listed as a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
GL.arrival: No official Greenland arrival procedure was found; a local funeral service or the family collects the coffin, and burial formalities are handled locally (confirm with the municipality). The Greenland health service refunds only an amount equal to one seated passenger ticket for patients who died while treated outside their home municipality; coffin costs fall on the estate.
GL.private_aviation: No official rule specific to private flights carrying human remains was found; confirm customs clearance with the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket.
GL.export: Not verified from Greenland sources: confirm with Landslaegeembedet, the airline and the destination country's consulate. Danish rules require a ligpas for bodies transported from Denmark to Greenland; for transport into Denmark the ligpas must be issued by the competent authority of the sending state.
GL.authority: Danish Patient Safety Authority (Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed) for transport from Denmark; Landslaegeembedet (Greenland chief medical officer); Naalakkersuisut

documents: Local death certificate (transcription into French civil status advised, done by the consulate)
Medical certificate / non-contagious disease certificate as required by the departure country
Embalming (soins de conservation) certificate where required at departure
Authorisation to transport the body issued by the French embassy or consulate (or a mortuary laissez-passer from a Strasbourg Agreement state)
Coffin closing / sealing report
Receiving funeral director and burial or cremation arrangements in Guadeloupe
GP.coffin: For air transport an airtight coffin (metal box) is mandatory under French rules (service-public.fr); in practice a soldered zinc lining inside a wooden coffin. A hermetic coffin cannot normally be cremated without being reopened, so plan cremation before departure.
GP.embalming: No general French embalming requirement for incoming bodies is stated in the official guidance; it is usually required by the departure country and by carriers. Confirm with the consulate.
GP.consular: The French embassy or consulate in the country of death issues the authorisation to transport the body to France (including overseas departments) and can transcribe the death certificate. France is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement, so a laissez-passer from another party state is accepted. From mainland France, no consulate is involved: the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed authorises transport to Guadeloupe.
GP.arrival: The receiving funeral director in Guadeloupe takes charge after customs and health formalities. French rules set burial no later than the 14th calendar day after death; how this applies to deaths abroad is not stated, so confirm with the funeral director and the prefecture of Guadeloupe.
GP.private_aviation: Same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The airtight zinc-lined coffin rule applies to any flight. Use an airport with customs (the main international airport) and arrange for the funeral director to meet the aircraft.
GP.export: To send a coffin out of Guadeloupe, the funeral director obtains authorisation from the prefect of Guadeloupe (the department where the coffin is closed), for EU, non-EU and mainland France destinations alike. An airtight metal coffin is mandatory for air transport. The destination country's consular requirements also apply.
GP.authority: French embassy or consulate abroad (entry); Prefect of Guadeloupe (exit)

documents: Original official death certificate issued by the local health authorities
Deceased's passport or national ID (DIP)
Embalming certificate
Non-infectious (non-contagious) disease certificate
Hermetically sealed coffin certificate
Burial transit permit from the country of death
Funeral home details and flight details (airline, date, route, e.g. Houston-Malabo)
Applicant's passport or ID
GQ.coffin: Hermetically sealed coffin required: the embassy asks for a certificate that the coffin is hermetically sealed. Zinc lining and outer case are not specified; a metal-lined sealed casket in a wooden outer case is the usual standard. Who witnesses the sealing is not published.
GQ.embalming: Required: an embalming certificate is a mandatory upload when the family wishes to repatriate the remains.
GQ.consular: Apply to the Equatorial Guinea embassy or consulate in the country of death (online application at the Washington embassy). The consular emergency team reviews the death certificate and repatriation authorisations and liaises with the funeral home for transit permits. Service is free. Equatorial Guinea is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
GQ.arrival: Clearance procedures at Malabo or Bata are not published. Arrange collection by a local funeral service in advance.
GQ.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. The embassy form asks for airline, date and route of the repatriation flight, so give the charter operator, date and route instead and confirm with the embassy that a private flight is acceptable. Land at an international airport (Malabo or Bata) with customs, immigration and health services.
GQ.export: Not officially published. Expect to need a death certificate, embalming and authorisation from the local authorities. Confirm with the consulate of the destination country.
GQ.authority: Embassy or consulate of Equatorial Guinea (consular section) in the country of death

documents: Medical certificate from the hospital or clinic stating the cause of death
Embalming certificate
Local death certificate
Medical certificate that the deceased had no communicable disease in the 6 months before death
Relative's authorisation for the transfer (at a consulate, KEP office or via gov.gr)
Exit permit from the country of death
Flight details to Greece
Apostille where required, Greek translations with the translator's signature certified by the consulate
Greek civil registry death certificate (printed by the consulate)
GR.coffin: The embalmed body is placed in a closed metal coffin with a 5 cm layer of absorbent material soaked in antiseptic and embalming fluid at the bottom. This goes inside an airtight wooden coffin and is wedged so it cannot move. If death was caused by a contagious disease, the body is also wrapped in a cover containing antiseptic. Sealing takes place in front of the consular authorities, by appointment.
GR.embalming: Mandatory: embalming according to scientific rules, certified by the competent authority.
GR.consular: The application is made in person at the Greek consulate with ID. The transfer certificate costs EUR 10 and is issued the same day once the file is complete. Death certificate copies are also listed at EUR 10 each. Greece has been a party to the Strasbourg Agreement since 1983 (Law 1315/1983), but the consular certificate is still the published route.
GR.arrival: The receiving Greek funeral director collects the coffin at the airport and arranges burial with the municipality. Burials in Greece normally take place within a month of death. For COVID-19 or other special cases, contact the Ministry of Health (ddy@moh.gov.gr).
GR.private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and 70-100 kg, so it must fit through the cargo door and into the cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. The coffin is sealed in front of the consul before departure and the seal must still be intact on arrival. A flight from outside the Schengen area must land at an airport with border and customs control.
GR.export: To send a body out of Greece, the death is registered at the local registry office (dimos), and the funeral director obtains a permit to remove the body, an embalming certificate and the deceased's passport. Local formalities usually take 8-10 days. The destination country's consular rules also apply.
GR.authority: Ministry of Health; Greek consular authorities abroad

documents: No published list for human remains; contact the Government of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands (GSGSSI) in Stanley
Entry is controlled under the Entry Control Ordinance 2022 (vessel booking notification and visitor permits)
Documents for the onward air leg are those of the Falkland Islands and the destination country
GS.coffin: No published casket rules for the territory. In practice the casket must meet the requirements of the ship operator and of the Falkland Islands / destination country for the onward flight.
GS.embalming: Not published; no embalming facilities are documented on the islands. Confirm with GSGSSI and the funeral director handling the onward journey.
GS.consular: UK Overseas Territory: no consulate. The Government of SGSSI (Government House, Stanley, Falkland Islands) and the UK FCDO are the contacts. Deaths entering the territory fall under Her/His Majesty's Coroner for South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, who sits in Stanley and applies the coroner law of England in modified form.
GS.arrival: There is no airport, so there is no air arrival clearance. Arrival by sea is subject to the Entry Control Ordinance 2022 and biosecurity rules. A body entering the territory (for example from a cruise ship) is dealt with by the Coroner for SGSSI, as South Georgia is then the first jurisdiction the body enters; contact GSGSSI and the Coroner in Stanley before any movement.
GS.private_aviation: Not possible: South Georgia has no airport or runway, and GSGSSI does not permit the use of aircraft, including helicopters. Transport is by ship (usually to/from the Falkland Islands, about 800 miles away), with the flight leg starting or ending in the Falklands.
GS.export: No published procedure. A death on or near South Georgia is handled with GSGSSI, the Coroner for SGSSI (sitting in Stanley) and the vessel operator; the body is carried by ship to the Falkland Islands or another port, from where the air repatriation follows that place's rules (in the Falklands: Coroner's no-objection, Order for Removal and Free From Infection Certificate).
GS.authority: Government of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands (Government House, Stanley); HM Coroner for South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands
