documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death (English or with a translation), unless the remains are embalmed
Embalming certificate where the body is embalmed
Consular Report of Death Abroad or Consular Mortuary Certificate from the US embassy if the deceased was a US citizen
Removal or export permit from the country of departure
Passport of the deceased and air waybill or flight manifest
Name and contact of the receiving licensed funeral home in Guam
GU.coffin: CDC requires all non-cremated remains to be fully contained in a leak-proof container (for example a casket with a leak-proof lining or a sealed metal transfer case). No territorial rule on zinc lining or witnessed sealing was found; the country of departure may impose a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin.
GU.embalming: Not required by US federal rules for entry, but embalmed remains are exempt from the CDC death-certificate requirement. Remains of a person who died of certain infectious diseases may need a CDC import permit unless embalmed. Most departure countries and airlines require embalming anyway.
GU.consular: No legalisation is required for entry. If a US citizen dies abroad, the US embassy or consulate can issue a Consular Report of Death Abroad and, where no death certificate exists, a Consular Mortuary Certificate. Foreign-language documents need an English translation.
GU.arrival: CBP clears the remains at the first US port of entry, with CDC requirements checked against the documents. Under 42 CFR 71.55 the remains must go directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory. Under Guam law (10 GCA 3230), a permit issued under the law of any state which accompanies a body brought into Guam for final disposition is the authority to dispose of it, but the Director of Public Health may order a particular form of burial or disposition given the cause of death.
GU.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. An international arrival into Guam must clear US Customs and Border Protection, so plan the flight to an airport where CBP clearance can be arranged in advance and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. A flight from the US mainland is a domestic flight and needs no CBP entry, but the state burial-transit permit must travel with the remains.
GU.export: Under 10 GCA 3230, no body may be buried, cremated or removed from Guam without a burial-transit permit issued by the Office of Vital Statistics (Department of Public Health and Social Services). The person first taking custody of the body must obtain it within 72 hours after death, and it is issued only after the death certificate has been filed. Permits for disposition outside Guam are issued only when the disposition complies with the Director's regulations. The destination consulate's requirements also apply.
GU.authority: US CDC and CBP (entry); Guam Office of Vital Statistics, Department of Public Health and Social Services (exit)

documents: Application form DH 2437 (Import of a Human Corpse) or the online e-form
Identity document of the applicant (original and copy)
Identity document of the deceased (original and copy)
Death certificate or medical certificate of the cause of death (original or certified copy)
Embalming certificate and autopsy report, if available
Translation into Chinese or English, certified by a consulate or notary, for documents in other languages
HK.coffin: Hong Kong does not publish a casket specification. The application asks whether the body is sealed in a robust leak-proof plastic bag and its infection risk category, and handling must follow the 'Precautions for Handling and Disposal of Dead Bodies' guideline. Use an IATA-compliant sealed casket for the flight.
HK.embalming: Not mandatory; the embalming certificate is submitted if available.
HK.consular: No consular transfer permit is required by Hong Kong. Documents not in Chinese or English must be translated and verified by the relevant consulate or a notary.
HK.arrival: Port Health Division Airport Section at HKIA (open 24 hours) checks the original documents and issues the import permit. Every imported death (except air-to-air transit) is reported to the Coroner, who may order a post-mortem at a public mortuary; a decision takes one to two working days. Burial needs authorisation from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department; cremation needs a Department of Health cremation permit and a booking with the department. Ashes need no import permit.
HK.private_aviation: The import permit is processed by the Port Health Division Airport Section at Hong Kong International Airport, so arrival at HKIA allows 24-hour processing. Transit air-to-air shipments need the PDF form sent by fax.
HK.export: The Deaths Registry of the Immigration Department issues the Permit for Removal of Dead Body from Hong Kong (Form 9) after the death is registered, using form SF/BDR/3. For overseas destinations, proof of import permission from the receiving country and the burial permit of the overseas cemetery are needed. Removal to the Mainland goes through the China Funeral Association's international body service centre. A licensed undertaker arranges transport.
HK.authority: Department of Health, Port Health Division

documents: Apostilled death certificate
Medical certificate, if the death occurred in a hospital
Embalming certificate (or cremation certificate for ashes)
Certificado de salida de restos mortales issued by the Honduran consulate (requested last, once the other documents are ready)
Transit permit from the country of death and passport or ID of the deceased
HN.coffin: Not specified by the consulate; local funeral directors use special caskets for international carriage (FCDO). Assume a hermetically sealed, airline-compliant casket.
HN.embalming: An embalming certificate is required for the consular exit certificate for a body; cremation certificate for ashes.
HN.consular: The Honduran consulate issues the Certificado de salida de restos mortales free of charge; at the Madrid consulate it is requested by email or in person without an appointment. The consulate does not register the death: a relative registers it with the RNP in Tegucigalpa using the apostilled death certificate. State-funded repatriation is possible only for families without resources, requested in person by a first- or second-degree relative, and only if the family has not already signed with a funeral home; it takes about 4-6 weeks.
HN.arrival: Customs and health clearance at the international airport of entry; a local funeral home collects. Local custom is burial within 24 hours (FCDO).
HN.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the originals travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once sealed) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. No specific Honduran rule for private flights carrying remains was found; land at an international airport with customs and health officers with the consular exit certificate and originals.
HN.export: Leaving Honduras: a local funeral director arranges the local death certificate (in Spanish), a certificate of embalming and a certificate permitting transfer of the remains, and supplies the special casket. In violent or suspicious deaths the National Civil Police involve the Ministerio Publico and an autopsy is required. Cold storage exists in Tegucigalpa and La Ceiba but is rare elsewhere. Otherwise release usually within a few days.
HN.authority: Honduran consulate (Secretaria de Relaciones Exteriores, SRECI); Secretariat of Health; Registro Nacional de las Personas (RNP)

documents: International death extract, certified for use in Croatia
Medical certificate of the cause of death stating it was not a contagious disease
Proof of the deceased's citizenship and passport (a Croatian passport is cancelled by the mission)
Approval for the transfer issued by the departure country
Transport details: flight number, airline, arrival airport, onward transport and the person receiving the body
For a foreign national buried in Croatia: written confirmation of the burial place from the cemetery or parish
HR.coffin: For air transport: a hermetically sealed metal coffin, or a hermetically sealed bag with a filter safety valve, placed inside a wooden coffin. If the death was caused by a listed infectious disease, a soldered metal coffin inside a wooden coffin is required, with the body wrapped in cloth soaked in disinfectant. On the aircraft the coffin goes in the cargo hold, separate from baggage, unless a special aircraft is used, in which case the cabin may be used.
HR.embalming: Not required by Croatian rules for entry as far as could be verified. The British embassy notes that embalming is not compulsory in Croatia but can be requested, especially for repatriation.
HR.consular: The Croatian embassy or consulate issues the sprovodnica on the official form. Before transport starts, the carrier must notify the mission in the country of departure by email or fax, with the transport consent, date and place of departure. No sprovodnica is needed for transit through Croatia. Croatia is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
HR.arrival: The receiving funeral director collects the coffin. Ashes need no sprovodnica: carry the crematorium's certificate and show it to the police on entry.
HR.private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and 70-100 kg, so it must fit through the cargo door and into the cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Croatian rules allow the passenger cabin only on a special aircraft; on an Elysium Jet flight the coffin always travels in the cargo hold, separate from baggage, and must meet the sealed coffin rules.
HR.export: To send a body out of Croatia, the death is registered at the local registry office, which issues the death certificate (an international multilingual version is available; it does not show the cause of death). The transport request must state the border crossing. A death examiner (coroner) issues permission to remove the body. The sprovodnica is issued by the sanitary inspector where the death was from an infectious disease or for exhumed remains. For air transport the body must be in a sealed metal coffin or sealed bag inside a wooden coffin. Non-infectious bodies not yet buried must be transported within 48 hours of death.
HR.authority: Croatian diplomatic missions (entry); sanitary inspectorate and local registry (exit)

documents: Death certificate issued by a Haitian consul
Burial permit from the place of death
Certified copy of the death certificate
Copy of the funeral home's health department registration and embalmer's licence
Copy of the complete funeral bill
Letter from the county health office that the deceased had no contagious disease, signed, notarised and authenticated
Letter on funeral home letterhead confirming embalming and a properly sealed coffin, signed, notarised and authenticated
Passport of the deceased (need not be current), flight itinerary and the name and address of the funeral home in Haiti
HT.coffin: A sealer (properly sealed) casket is required; a wood-base air tray is acceptable.
HT.embalming: Mandatory, certified by a notarised and authenticated letter from the funeral home.
HT.consular: The consular section of the Embassy of Haiti in Washington (or a Haitian consulate) issues the death certificate for transport after reviewing the file; the Washington fee is USD 160 (money order or credit card). Other consulates may differ.
HT.arrival: The remains are released to the named funeral home in Haiti, which handles customs and burial. Haitian civil death certificates do not show the cause of death. Confirm timing with the receiving funeral home.
HT.private_aviation: No official Haitian rule specific to private flights carrying human remains was found. The security situation can disrupt flights and airport operations in Haiti, so check current aviation notices (NOTAMs) and the arrival airport's status before planning, and make sure a funeral home and handling agent can receive the casket. The consular death certificate and originals travel with the casket.
HT.export: Leaving Haiti, the next of kin (or a funeral director with a letter of authorisation) registers the death with the Civil Registry (Etat Civil); the funeral home provides the death certificate, an embalming certificate and a certificate permitting transfer of the remains, and meets the destination's requirements (for the US, CDC leak-proof container rules). Post-mortems are carried out by court-appointed forensic doctors.
HT.authority: Embassy of Haiti consular section and Haitian consulates; Ministere de la Sante Publique et de la Population

documents: Foreign death certificate (official Hungarian translation likely needed; confirm with the consulate)
Medical certificate of the cause of death
Transport permit issued by the Hungarian consular officer
Embalming certificate where required by the departure country
Passport of the deceased
HU.coffin: A double coffin is mandatory for every transport from abroad into Hungary. For air transport, or any transport to or from abroad, a metal coffin must be used inside the transport coffin. The coffin must be tightly closed and watertight.
HU.embalming: Not specifically required by Hungarian law for incoming bodies. Preservation is optional in Hungary, at the family's request. The departure country or airline usually requires embalming.
HU.consular: The Hungarian consular officer issues the permit to transport a body into Hungary, applying Hungarian domestic transport rules. Hungary is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement. Fees and processing times were not published in the sources checked; confirm with the consulate.
HU.arrival: At the destination, after notice from the cemetery operator, the public health authority inspects the shipment and withdraws and keeps the transport permit. For deaths in Hungary, coffin burial must normally take place within 96 hours of the death certificate, or within 15 days if the body is kept refrigerated. How this applies to bodies from abroad should be confirmed locally.
HU.private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and 70-100 kg, so it must fit through the cargo door and into the cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Hungary requires a metal inner coffin for any air transport. A flight from outside the Schengen area must land at an airport with border and customs control.
HU.export: Transporting a body abroad from Hungary needs a permit from the district office (járási hivatal) acting as the public health authority for the place of death. The application states the deceased's details, cause and date of death, route, vehicle, mode of transport and escort, and the permit sets the transport conditions, which are checked before departure. A metal coffin inside the transport coffin is mandatory for air transport or transport abroad. The destination country's consular rules also apply.
HU.authority: Hungarian consular officer (entry); district office acting as public health authority (exit)

documents: Doctor's statement of the death from the country of origin (Surat Uraian Kematian), presented to Customs on arrival
Export permit from the authorities of the country of death
Embalming and sealing certificates if required by the airline or departure country
Passport of the deceased
Air waybill
ID.coffin: Customs exempts from import duty a coffin or other container used only to hold or transport a body and sized for one body. No national specification on sealing or zinc lining was found in the official sources checked; airlines usually require a hermetically sealed coffin in an outer case. Confirm with the airline and the Indonesian embassy.
ID.embalming: No official Indonesian rule on embalming for incoming remains was found in the sources checked. Airlines and the departure country often require it; confirm with the Indonesian embassy or consulate.
ID.consular: Indonesian embassies and consulates assist with the paperwork for Indonesian nationals. The documents they request, and whether legalisation or an apostille is needed, were not published in the official sources checked; confirm with the Indonesian embassy or consulate.
ID.arrival: The airline or shipping agent informs the port health office of the arriving body; health quarantine officers verify the health documents and inspect the shipment, and can take quarantine action if there is a public health risk. To obtain the import duty exemption, the applicant presents the doctor's statement of the death to Customs on arrival; the exemption is free of charge and Customs decides within at most 14 working days of a complete application. Cargo handling fees may still apply. The receiving funeral service collects the coffin.
ID.private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights was found. Port health inspects arriving bodies at the airport, so arrive at an international airport with customs and port health and have the handling agent notify both in advance.
ID.export: Leaving Indonesia, the death is registered at the local civil registry (death certificate, Akta Kematian, which can take a few days). Permission to remove the body is issued by the Port Health Authority or other relevant authorities, on presentation of the death certificate and the deceased's passport. Police may order a post-mortem as part of a legal investigation. Confirm the destination country's requirements with its embassy.
ID.authority: Ministry of Health port health (Balai Kekarantinaan Kesehatan); Directorate General of Customs and Excise; Indonesian embassy or consulate

documents: Foreign death certificate (with translation if not in English)
Permission to remove the body from the country of death
Embalming certificate if required by the departure country or airline
Passport of the deceased
IE.coffin: No Irish import standard for the coffin was found in the official sources checked. International transport usually requires a hermetically sealed, zinc-lined coffin set by the departure country and the airline; a zinc-lined coffin may not be suitable for cremation, so check with the Irish funeral director and crematorium.
IE.embalming: Not required by Irish law for import as far as could be verified. Usually required by the departure country or airline.
IE.consular: The Department of Foreign Affairs and Irish embassies can help with local procedures and documentation and provide English-speaking local undertakers, but cannot pay for the return of the body, the funeral or relatives' travel. Repatriations take on average 10-14 days, often longer, depending on the formalities of the country of death. Ireland is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
IE.arrival: The Irish funeral director receives the coffin. If the death abroad was unexplained or suspicious, the family may request further examination of the remains by the coroner's office on return to Ireland (Dublin coroner: coroners@dublincity.ie).
IE.private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and 70-100 kg, so it must fit through the cargo door and into the cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Flights from outside the Common Travel Area should land at an airport with customs facilities.
IE.export: Leaving Ireland, the coroner for the district where the body lies is notified before the body is moved abroad and, if satisfied, issues a removal order, usually to the funeral director. The destination country's embassy sets the other documents (typically embalming certificate, passport, funeral director's declaration, entry permit and any notarisation or apostille) and the coffin standard; confirm with it and with the airline.
IE.authority: Department of Foreign Affairs (assistance); coroner (exit and unnatural deaths)

documents: Death certificate of the country of death (confirm authentication with the Israeli mission)
Copies of the passport or ID of the deceased and of the next of kin
Body transfer form signed by the next of kin
Commitment from a licensed Israeli burial society (Chevra Kadisha or other licensed burial company)
Certificate of preservation (preservative injection or dry ice packing)
Israeli consular permit for transfer of the body for burial
IL.coffin: The Israeli mission sources checked do not set a casket construction standard; the container is set by the departure country, the airline and the Israeli burial society. Confirm the container with the burial society before the flight.
IL.embalming: Israeli missions ask for a certificate that a preservative was injected into the body or that it was packed in dry ice. Jewish practice generally avoids embalming, so dry ice is often used where the departure country and carrier allow it.
IL.consular: The Israeli embassy or consulate issues the permit for transfer of bodies for burial in Israel, usually by appointment; no permit is required for ashes. Missions ask for a body transfer form signed by the next of kin, the burial company's commitment, the preservation certificate and copies of the passports or IDs of the deceased and the next of kin. Missions are not authorised to recommend funeral firms. Fees were not published in the sources checked; confirm with the mission.
IL.arrival: The coffin arrives at Ben Gurion Airport and is collected by the licensed burial society or its funeral service, which arranges a quick burial. Only people of the Jewish faith may be buried in Jewish cemeteries; civil burial areas exist.
IL.pouch: Accepted in practice: a human remains pouch in a combination tray can be used as the transport container, provided the departure country, the funeral home and the carrier allow it and the Israeli burial society agrees before the flight. No Israeli official text on the container was found.
IL.private_aviation: No rule specific to remains on private aircraft was found. The private flight lands at Ben Gurion, clears Israeli security and customs, and the burial society must be arranged to meet the aircraft. Check current airport and airspace notices, as Ben Gurion operations can be disrupted.
IL.export: Leaving Israel: the Ministry of the Interior issues the death certificate in Hebrew. If police request an autopsy it is done only at the National Centre of Forensic Medicine in Tel Aviv, needs next-of-kin consent or a court order, and the body is usually released within a couple of days. Without an autopsy no cause of death appears on the certificate; the forensic centre and Ministry of Health may review other documents in exceptional cases. A local funeral director handles the export paperwork with the destination funeral director.
IL.authority: Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs (embassies and consulates) with a licensed Israeli burial society

documents: Death certificate from the country of death, with certified English translation if not in English
Permission to remove the body issued by the competent authority of the country of death (laissez-passer, coroner's out-of-jurisdiction order or equivalent)
Embalming and non-contagious disease certificates where the departure country issues them
Passport or ID of the deceased
Notification to the Isle of Man coroner (arranged by the Manx funeral director)
IM.coffin: No Manx coffin specification was found in official sources. Airlines and the departure country normally require a sealed, zinc-lined coffin in an outer wooden case for international air transport; confirm with the receiving funeral director.
IM.embalming: No Manx embalming rule for incoming bodies was found; the departure country's rules and the carrier's requirements apply.
IM.consular: No Isle of Man consular step exists (it is a Crown Dependency; the UK represents it abroad). British embassies and consulates can advise families on the local procedure in the country of death.
IM.arrival: The coroner within whose jurisdiction the body will finally lie must be notified; the coroner then decides whether an inquest is necessary. After any coronial process, the registrar issues a burial order, or the coroner issues a cremation certificate. A local funeral director collects the coffin.
IM.private_aviation: Fly into Ronaldsway (Isle of Man Airport) with customs available and the receiving funeral director meeting the aircraft. Human remains on a private flight need the same papers as airline cargo, carried with the coffin. The coffin (about 2.2 m, 70-100 kg zinc-lined) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
IM.export: The coroner must be given written notice of any body being taken out of the Isle of Man and issues an Out of Isle of Man Order once satisfied with the result of any enquiries ordered. The death must normally be registered within 5 days at a civil registry office on the basis of the doctor's certificate of cause of death or the coroner's finding.
IM.authority: Coroner of Inquests (High Bailiff), Isle of Man; Civil Registry

documents: Embalming certificate stating the body is embalmed and in a hermetically sealed (airtight and waterproof) casket
Death certificate stating the cause of death (or true copy), with English translation
No-objection certificate (NOC) from the Indian embassy, high commission or consulate
Cancelled passport of the deceased
Certificate of packaging per WHO guidelines
Consignee certificate that the casket contains only the named remains
Municipal or government certificate from the country of origin (endorsed by the Indian mission) with name, age, place, date and cause of death and confirming the sealing
Non-communicable disease certificate and legal heir's consent, as Indian missions request
IN.coffin: Body in a zinc or other metal shell with all joints soldered to seal it hermetically, placed in a strong teak or hardwood coffin, inside a zinc- or tin-lined wooden packing case. Unembalmed remains (drowning, severe burns) go in a hermetically sealed container; the APHO may require extra packing. The package must not be opened in transit.
IN.embalming: An embalming certificate is required. Bodies not embalmed (for example after drowning or severe burns) must be in a hermetically sealed container, and the Airport Health Officer may impose extra packing.
IN.consular: The Indian embassy, high commission or consulate in the country of death issues the no-objection certificate (NOC) after local formalities, cancels the passport and endorses the certificate of the local municipal or government authority. MEA guidance also lists a clinical death certificate, embalming certificate, non-communicable disease certificate and power of attorney/consent from the legal heir. If there is no Indian mission in that country, the Airport Health Officer may waive the NOC. Health clearance is managed through the Ministry of Health's eCARe (e-Clearance for Afterlife Remains) portal.
IN.arrival: Remains are kept at a separate designated place at the airport and cannot leave until the Airport Health Officer authorises removal in writing; the consignee then disposes of them under local municipal rules. Bodies of people who died of yellow fever, plague, anthrax, glanders or other notified diseases may not be brought in.
IN.private_aviation: The same APHO health clearance applies at any Indian international airport, including the 48-hour email notice to the Airport Health Officer. Flight permissions for a foreign private aircraft are separate; confirm with the handling agent.
IN.export: Export needs prior written permission from the competent authority of the destination country, and from the District Magistrate, Deputy Commissioner, Chief Presidency Magistrate or Coroner for the place of death. The death is registered locally and the death certificate is normally issued 10-15 working days after registration. The body must be embalmed before repatriation. Police release the body after a post-mortem in unnatural deaths. UK guidance says local formalities generally take about two weeks.
IN.authority: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare - Airport Health Organisation (APHO); Ministry of External Affairs (Indian missions)

documents: Foreign death certificate, authenticated or apostilled in the country of death
Iraqi Civil Status ID and Nationality Certificate, or Unified National Card, of the deceased
ID of the relative reporting the death
Iraqi death certificate application filed online (icass.mofa.gov.iq) with consular appointment
Written request from the next of kin naming the entry point (airport) for the body
Medical certificate that the deceased was free of COVID-19 (requested by the Los Angeles consulate)
Burial or transit permit and health certificate from the country of death (confirm the current list with the consulate)
IQ.coffin: No Iraqi rule on casket construction was found in official sources. In practice a hermetically sealed, metal-lined casket in an outer wooden case is expected for air transport; confirm with the consulate and the airline or operator.
IQ.embalming: No official Iraqi entry rule on embalming was found. Many departure countries and airlines require it; Muslim families may ask to avoid it. Confirm with the Iraqi consulate.
IQ.consular: The Iraqi embassy or consulate registers the death (the Los Angeles consulate charges USD 15 to authenticate the foreign death certificate, plus late penalties if registered more than 30 days after the death) and handles the request to transport the body for burial in Iraq. The Iraqi Embassy in Washington lists a USD 3,200 fee for transporting the remains of Arabs or foreigners for burial in Iraq. The Los Angeles consulate also asks for a medical certificate that the deceased was free of COVID-19; confirm the current list with the consulate.
IQ.arrival: The body enters through the airport named in the request, where it is cleared by Iraqi authorities and released to the family or a funeral service. Muslim burial takes place as soon as possible.
IQ.private_aviation: The Iraqi consular approval is tied to a named entry point, so the private flight must land at that airport (for example Baghdad, Najaf, Basra or Erbil) and the operator must hold Iraqi landing and overflight permits. Check current conflict-zone notices for Iraqi airspace before planning.
IQ.export: Leaving Iraq is governed by the Funerals Transfer Law No. 52 of 1967. The death is registered in Iraq (certificate in Arabic showing the cause of death); an autopsy is usually required outside the Kurdistan Region and carried out unless the cause is very clear inside it. Bodies are usually moved to the Baghdad funeral office at Bab Almoazam, next to the Institute of Forensic Medicine. Iraqi authorities require a No Objection letter from the deceased's embassy, and a consular officer witnesses the sealing of the casket and legalises the death certificate.
IQ.authority: Iraqi Ministry of Foreign Affairs (embassies and consulates)

documents: Laissez-passer for the corpse from the country of death (Strasbourg Agreement states)
Certificate on the packaging of the body (Regulation 618/2018, art. 3)
Doctor's certificate stating whether the deceased had a contagious disease or other infection risk (art. 3)
Death certificate, with English translation where needed (legalisation for non-Strasbourg origins to be confirmed with the Icelandic embassy)
IS.coffin: Regulation 618/2018 (art. 2): the body must be placed in an airtight and watertight container inside a sturdy coffin and secured so that it cannot move. In practice this means a sealed zinc-lined inner coffin in a wooden coffin. Iceland does not publish who must witness the sealing; the departure country's rules apply.
IS.embalming: Iceland's regulation does not require embalming for an incoming body; follow the departure country's and the airline's rules.
IS.consular: From Strasbourg Agreement states no Icelandic consular step is needed. From other countries, no Icelandic consular permit is published; ask the Icelandic embassy or consulate whether legalised documents are required. Iceland's Foreign Ministry consular service assists families of Icelandic citizens who die abroad.
IS.arrival: Customs clearance at the arrival airport (normally Keflavik). If an incoming body has no certificate, it is handled under the procedures of the Chief Epidemiologist (sottvarnalaeknir) together with the district chief physicians. A body that may carry a notifiable disease is transported and kept under the Chief Epidemiologist's procedures. A local funeral director collects the coffin; Reykjavik's cemeteries run the main mortuary and two crematoria.
IS.private_aviation: Fly to an Icelandic airport with customs (Keflavik, or Reykjavik for general aviation, to be confirmed with the handler) and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft. The same packaging and medical certificates apply as for airline cargo, and the coffin must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
IS.export: For Strasbourg Agreement destinations, Iceland's declared competent authority for the laissez-passer is the District Medical Officer (in Reykjavik, the Reykjavik Medical Office of Health), who may authorise staff doctors at health centres and hospitals to act (declaration of 4 February 1983). The body leaves in an airtight, watertight container inside a sturdy coffin with the packaging and medical certificates required by Regulation 618/2018. A doctor certifies the death and the National Registry registers it (Icelandic death certificates do not show the cause of death); a police inquiry or post-mortem can delay the release. Exhumation for transfer abroad needs a permit from the Chief Epidemiologist.
IS.authority: Ministry of Health and the Chief Epidemiologist (Directorate of Health); District Medical Officer for the laissez-passer

documents: Death certificate (long form, with cause of death), apostilled and with full Italian translation; some consulates ask for two
Health authority certificate that the death was not from a contagious disease and that the remains were treated per local law
Notarised funeral director's affidavit attesting compliance with the Italian Mortuary Police Regulation (DPR 285/1990)
Repatriation request signed by the next of kin with ID; consular data sheet
Deceased's Italian passport (cancelled) or proof of identity/citizenship
Mortuary passport (passaporto mortuario) issued by the Italian consulate after municipal clearance, or by the departure authority for Berlin Agreement states
IT.coffin: DPR 285/1990 art. 30 requires a double coffin for international transport outside the Berlin Agreement: an outer metal case of zinc at least 0.660 mm (or lead 1.5 mm) hermetically sealed by continuous welding, and a solid wood coffin with boards at least 25 mm thick, screwed lid, absorbent biodegradable material at the bottom and metal bands. The consulate tells the funeral director when the coffin may be sealed.
IT.embalming: DPR 285/1990 art. 32 requires antiputrefaction treatment (at least 500 cc of formalin) from April to September, and in other months when the journey exceeds 24 hours or starts more than 48 hours after death; embalmed bodies are exempt. Consulates ask for a certificate that the remains were treated according to local law.
IT.consular: The Italian consulate in the country of death receives the file (apostilled and translated documents), requests the nulla osta from the municipality of burial, and only then issues the mortuary passport. A consular fee applies (Consular Fee Table art. 66H). The Miami consulate advises allowing about 3 weeks.
IT.arrival: The Italian funeral director (impresa funebre) receives the coffin at the airport and takes it by road to the cemetery or crematorium authorised by the municipality. Cremation needs a separate municipal authorisation.
IT.private_aviation: The mortuary passport and municipal clearance must be in hand before departure; the documents travel with the coffin. The Italian Embassy in Washington states that after arrival at the first Italian airport the remains must continue to their destination by land, as air transport within Italy is not allowed, so land at the airport closest to the place of burial. Use an airport of entry with customs and arrange for the funeral director to meet the aircraft.
IT.export: To leave Italy for a Berlin Agreement state the body travels with a mortuary passport (DPR 285/1990 art. 27). For other countries, the transport authorisation is requested with the entry clearance (nulla osta) of the destination country's consulate and a local health authority (ASL) certificate of compliance with the art. 30 coffin rules (art. 29). Italian law requires a basic preservation treatment for repatriation abroad; partial embalming needs the mayor's authorisation and may cause delay. The funeral director completes the transfer of remains certificate. Local formalities can take up to 2 weeks.
IT.authority: Italian consulate abroad; municipality (comune) of burial; Ministry of Health rules (DPR 285/1990)

documents: Death registration/certificate from the country of death, with translation if needed
Permission to remove the body from the country of death (coroner or equivalent authority)
Application to the Jersey Coroner for permission to bring the body to Jersey (form from the Viscount's Department Court Services Team, usually completed by the funeral director)
Any foreign post-mortem report, if one was carried out
JE.coffin: No Jersey coffin specification was found in official sources; the departure country and carrier normally require a sealed, zinc-lined coffin for international air transport.
JE.embalming: No Jersey embalming rule for incoming bodies was found; the departure country's rules apply.
JE.consular: No Jersey consular step (Crown Dependency). For deaths outside the British Isles, the British consulate in that country can help the next of kin.
JE.arrival: The Coroner may hold an inquest or order a post-mortem on arrival, taking into account any post-mortem abroad. The funeral date should not be fixed until the Coroner has decided. A Jersey funeral director collects the coffin.
JE.private_aviation: Fly into Jersey Airport with the Coroner's permission already granted and the Jersey funeral director meeting the aircraft. Human remains on a private flight need the same papers as airline cargo. The coffin must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
JE.export: Permission must be obtained from the Coroner before a body can be removed from Jersey in all cases. The Jersey funeral director completes the application, which requires a copy of the death certificate from the Superintendent Registrar (death registered within 5 days) and any further evidence requested, such as the passport. The funeral director must arrange reception in the destination and transit jurisdictions. Do not make travel arrangements before permission is given.

documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death (English translation if needed)
Embalming certificate (except where embalming is prohibited for religious reasons)
Permit from the Medical Officer (Health) of the parish of entry, applied for in writing on the prescribed form with fee
Statement that the body is in a hermetically sealed casket, if death was from a quarantinable communicable disease
Free-from-infection certificate, coroner or post-mortem report where applicable, ID of the deceased and the transit permit of the country of death (as listed by the Jamaican Consulate in Toronto)
JM.coffin: Embalmed remains in a leak-proof container (puncture-resistant and sealed) if the cause of death is not a quarantinable communicable disease; a hermetically sealed casket, with documentation of the sealing, if it is (e.g. Ebola, cholera, infectious tuberculosis, plague, yellow fever, SARS). The casket should travel in an air tray or a compartment separate from baggage.
JM.embalming: Required, with an embalming certificate, except where embalming is prohibited for religious reasons.
JM.consular: No Jamaican consular document was found in the Ministry of Health guidelines. Jamaican missions advise using a funeral home in the country of death and a registered Jamaican funeral home with a licensed embalmer, which obtains the permit. A death certificate in another language needs an English translation.
JM.arrival: The airline or importer notifies the Medical Officer (Health) or Chief Public Health Inspector and the Quarantine Officer at least 24 hours before arrival (airline, flight, point of entry, date and time, name of the deceased). The remains are stored at the airport apart from food; the permit is presented to Customs for clearance and the funeral home collects. The Medical Officer (Health) may order detention, disinfection or other measures if contamination is suspected. Unclaimed remains are stored at the consignee's expense.
JM.private_aviation: The parish health permit must be obtained before arrival and the 24-hour arrival notification applies to any flight. Land at an international airport with customs and health officers and present the permit to Customs on arrival; confirm the airport with the handling agent.
JM.export: Leaving Jamaica, the death must be registered within 5 days unless the coroner is investigating; a post-mortem is always carried out after a sudden or suspected violent death, and the full registration process usually takes about 6 months (up to 2 years), so ask early which document the destination accepts. Repatriation needs a certificate permitting the transfer of the remains and an embalming certificate. Jamaican missions state that only registered funeral homes with a licensed embalmer can obtain a transit permit from the public health department (Kingston and St Andrew or St James).
JM.authority: Ministry of Health and Wellness (Environmental Health Unit); parish Medical Officer (Health)

documents: Official foreign death certificate, attested by the Jordanian embassy in the country of death
Certified Arabic translation of the death certificate
Medical certificate of non-contagious disease (expected; confirm with the consulate)
Embalming and sealed casket certificates (expected; confirm with the consulate)
Deceased's passport or Jordanian ID
JO.coffin: No official Jordanian import standard was found. Use a hermetically sealed, zinc-lined casket in an outer wooden case meeting airline requirements; confirm with the Jordanian consulate.
JO.embalming: Not published officially for incoming remains; confirm with the Jordanian consulate.
JO.consular: The Jordanian embassy or consulate attests the foreign death certificate; the death of a Jordanian can be registered with the Civil Status and Passports Department or at a Jordanian embassy (JD1 fee, extra JD10 after 7 days).
JO.arrival: Detailed arrival rules for incoming remains are not published; confirm customs and health clearance with the consulate and handling agent. For deaths in Jordan, law requires burial within 24 hours, extendable to 72 hours with a Ministry of Health permit if remains are kept in a suitable facility (gov.uk). Cremation is not permitted in Jordan.
JO.private_aviation: No official rule specific to private flights carrying human remains was found. Plan arrival at an international airport (e.g. Amman Queen Alia) with customs and health staff, and confirm clearance with the handling agent.
JO.export: The hospital issues a notification of death; the Civil Status and Passports Department issues the death certificate (Arabic; English version on request, without cause of death). Deaths outside hospital require an autopsy (usually within 2 to 3 days). Jordanian authorities require a no-objection letter from the deceased's embassy and written next-of-kin consent. Embalming and sealing requirements for exit are not published officially. Cremation is not permitted. The authorities must be told if the deceased had an infectious condition such as hepatitis or HIV.
JO.authority: Jordanian embassy/consulate abroad; Civil Status and Passports Department; Ministry of Health

documents: Foreign death certificate (original) with Japanese translation (confirm with the municipality or consulate)
Embalming certificate from the funeral home abroad (usually requested by airlines)
Any document required by the Japanese embassy or consulate (for Japanese nationals; confirm)
Deceased's passport
Death notification (shibo todoke) filed with a Japanese municipality, which then issues the burial or cremation permit
JP.coffin: No Japanese entry specification for the casket has been published. In practice airlines require an IATA-compliant, metal-lined sealed casket for a body.
JP.embalming: Not required by a published Japanese entry rule, but embalming certificates are normally requested by airlines for transport. Japanese law forbids burial or cremation within 24 hours of death.
JP.consular: No Japanese consular step for an incoming casket is published in the official sources reviewed. For a Japanese national, ask the Japanese embassy or consulate in the country of death which documents and translations it requires; for foreign nationals, check with the municipality where cremation or burial will take place.
JP.arrival: The casket is cleared as air cargo. Under the Graveyards and Burial Act, burial or cremation needs a permit from the mayor of the municipality that received the death notification, and cannot take place within 24 hours of death. Cremation is the norm in Japan; burial space is scarce.
JP.private_aviation: Foreign-registered business jets need permission from the Japan Civil Aviation Bureau for paid passenger carriage into Japan and for landings at non-designated airports. The standard filing deadline is 10 days before the flight; since June 2023 it is 3 days for sightseeing flights, and the Minister can accept late applications when there is unavoidable cause. Thirty-six designated airports need no individual landing permission.
JP.export: The Australian Embassy in Tokyo states that no Japanese national or local law governs the export of human remains; a casket travels as ordinary freight, and shipping companies usually require a metal-lined casket. The death must be notified to the city, ward or town office within 7 days (gov.uk). Embalming or cremation cannot start until 24 hours after death. A local funeral director issues the embalming certificate, and a repatriation company certifies that the coffin contains only the remains; the destination country sets any further paperwork. Final arrangements are normally needed within about a week because cold storage is scarce.
JP.authority: Municipal office (city, ward, town) for burial and cremation permits; Japanese embassy or consulate abroad

documents: Proof of Kenyan nationality of the deceased (passport, ID card or birth certificate) where applicable
Certified copy of the death certificate
Locally issued burial and/or transit permit (in the UK: Out of England certificate)
Letter from the local health authority that the death was not from a contagious disease
Letter from the funeral director confirming and describing the embalming
No objection letter from the Kenyan embassy or high commission
KE.coffin: Kenyan missions recommend a sealable casket; the Kenyan Embassy in Washington recommends a metal, hermetically sealable casket. Airline packaging rules also apply. No witnessing of the sealing by a Kenyan official is required by the published checklists.
KE.embalming: Required: missions ask for a funeral director's letter confirming embalming; the London High Commission asks that it state embalming in line with ICAO and international guidelines.
KE.consular: The Kenyan mission issues a no objection letter for transport of the remains (the London High Commission sends it to the next of kin). The Washington and Madrid missions charge no fee; the Kenya Embassy in Spain states one day once documents are complete. Names and dates must match on all documents, or approvals are delayed. Not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement 1973, so a mortuary laissez-passer alone is not enough.
KE.arrival: Remains are cleared by customs and port health at the arrival airport and released to the family or their funeral home. Ministry of Health clearance was specifically required for COVID-19 related remains (2021 protocol); confirm whether it still applies to infectious-disease deaths.
KE.private_aviation: No Kenyan rules specific to private flights carrying remains were published. Land at an international airport with customs and port health (Nairobi JKIA or Mombasa) and carry the original no objection letter and documents with the casket.
KE.export: To send a body out of Kenya, the death is registered with the Civil Registration Office or a Huduma centre (burial permit, death certificate in English showing the cause). Polish consular guidance lists the Kenyan documents usually issued: burial permit from local authorities, certificate of no infectious disease and embalming certificate. Deaths outside hospital are reported to police and a post-mortem may be needed, which can delay release. The destination country's embassy may need to issue its own entry authorisation.
KE.authority: Kenyan embassy or high commission in the country of death; Ministry of Health (port health) on arrival

documents: Death certificate from the country of death, with translation (confirm with consulate)
Embalming certificate (expected; confirm)
Certificate that the death was not caused by a contagious disease (expected; confirm)
Zinc sealing certificate (expected; confirm)
Export permit from the country of death
Passport of the deceased
KG.coffin: Not published officially for entry. A sealed zinc coffin with a sealing report is required for bodies leaving Kyrgyzstan, and the same standard should be expected on entry; confirm with the Kyrgyz consulate.
KG.embalming: Not published officially; embalming is expected for international transport. Confirm with the Kyrgyz consulate.
KG.consular: Kyrgyzstan is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Contact the Kyrgyz embassy or consulate in the country of death about consular certification, legalisation or apostille and Kyrgyz or Russian translations.
KG.arrival: Not published officially. Expect customs and sanitary clearance at the arrival airport (normally Bishkek or Osh) and handover to a local funeral service. There is no cremation service in Kyrgyzstan.
KG.private_aviation: No official rule specific to human remains on private aircraft was found. Plan arrival at an international airport with customs, border and sanitary-quarantine control, and have the handling agent confirm clearance of the coffin in advance.
KG.export: The death is registered with the civil registry (ZAGS), which issues a death certificate in Russian and Kyrgyz in 3 to 5 business days. Leaving Kyrgyzstan requires the local medical and civil death certificates, a certificate permitting transfer of the remains and a zinc coffin sealing report. Local formalities normally take around 7 days.
KG.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kyrgyzstan (consular service); State Registry Service (ZAGS) for deaths in Kyrgyzstan

documents: Original death certificate
Letter from the funeral home
Hospital letter confirming natural death, no contagious disease and that the body is safe to transport
Airline ticket with travel itinerary
Embassy processing fee
Any further document the embassy handling the case requests (confirm)
KH.coffin: No official Cambodian casket standard was found. Use a hermetically sealed, zinc-lined coffin in an outer wooden case per airline/IATA rules.
KH.embalming: Not specified by the Cambodian embassy checklist reviewed (Canberra asks for a hospital safe-to-transport letter); embalming is in any case required by most departure countries and airlines. Confirm with the embassy.
KH.consular: The Royal Embassy of Cambodia processes the file for a processing fee (amount not published; ask the embassy). The Canberra embassy lists the original death certificate, funeral home letter, hospital letter and air ticket with itinerary; no processing time is published. Requirements may vary by embassy.
KH.arrival: No official arrival procedure was published. Customs clear the coffin at Phnom Penh or Siem Reap and the family or local funeral service collects it; present the embassy letter on arrival.
KH.private_aviation: No Cambodian rule specific to private flights carrying remains was found. Land at an international airport with customs and health staff and agree the clearance with the handling agent, carrying the embassy letter on board.
KH.export: Leaving Cambodia, the funeral director obtains the supporting documents with the deceased's embassy; the Khmer death certificate can take four to six weeks, while local repatriation formalities can take up to seven days (gov.uk). Post-mortems are not carried out in Cambodia. Refrigerated storage is scarce and costly, and authorities may cremate within 24 hours on public health grounds. Cremation requires Ministry of Health permission.
KH.authority: Royal Embassy of Cambodia in the country of death

documents: Death certificate (original or certified copy; the London High Commission asks for the original)
Statement of death
Burial / transit permit from the place of death
Embalming certificate or embalmer's affidavit
Letter of non-contagious disease (free from infection) from the local health authority
Coffin sealing certificate
Funeral home letter: only remains in the casket, hermetically sealed container in an all-wood outer case, consignee name and contacts, flight details and arrival time
Proof of identity / citizenship of the deceased (passport bio page or birth certificate)
Copies notarised (London High Commission guidance)
KN.coffin: The body must be in a hermetically sealed container placed inside an all-wood outer shipping container, and a coffin sealing certificate is required. The sealing is done and certified by the funeral home at departure; no witnessing by a Kittitian official is described.
KN.embalming: Embalming is required: an embalming certificate (or embalmer's affidavit) is part of the file.
KN.consular: Documents go to a Saint Kitts and Nevis mission (the Toronto consulate asks for them at least 14 days before departure; the London High Commission asks for notarised copies sent to the local funeral director). On receipt, the Chief Medical Officer issues a letter permitting the remains to be shipped into the Federation. No Strasbourg laissez-passer arrangement applies.
KN.arrival: The person accompanying the remains presents the original documents on arrival and all contents must be declared to Customs. The local funeral director, who processed the file with the Ministry of Health, collects the casket. No legal burial deadline was found in official sources.
KN.private_aviation: No rules specific to private flights were found. The Chief Medical Officer's permission letter must be issued before departure and the casket must clear Customs at a port of entry; the flight details and arrival time are part of the file, so give the exact private flight details to the funeral home.
KN.export: Leaving Saint Kitts and Nevis: the death is registered with the Registrar General (St Kitts) or Registrar General Department (Nevis); the certificate (English, with cause of death) is usually issued within 2 days of a post-mortem. The local funeral director provides the embalming certificate and a permit to transfer the remains. Post-mortems are common for foreign nationals and can take 3-5 days or more because the medical examiner is based in Barbados.
KN.authority: Ministry of Health, Chief Medical Officer (via Basseterre Health Centre)

documents: Death certificate or post-mortem (autopsy) certificate stating the cause of death (Quarantine Act Enforcement Rule, Art. 19)
Copy of the air waybill (or bill of lading for sea transport) (Art. 19)
Embalming certificate: legally required when death was due to a quarantinable infectious disease; Korean embassies also list it for all repatriated bodies
Any further document the quarantine station chief requests to rule out a quarantinable infectious disease (Art. 19)
Original passport of the deceased (Korean embassy guidance)
Korean or English translation of foreign documents, with Korean consular confirmation or apostille (embassy guidance)
KR.coffin: For deaths from a quarantinable infectious disease, the quarantine station refuses entry unless the body is embalmed and sealed in an impermeable coffin, or cremated (Quarantine Act, Art. 25(2)). For other deaths the law sets no coffin specification; use an airline (IATA) compliant hermetically sealed casket in an outer case.
KR.embalming: Embalming certificate is legally required only when death was caused by a quarantinable infectious disease (Enforcement Rule Art. 19(2)); in practice Korean embassies (Spain, Poland) list an embalming certificate for every body repatriated to Korea.
KR.consular: The Korean embassy or consulate in the country of death performs consular confirmation of the foreign documents (Warsaw embassy) and, in Spain, notarises the Korean translations of Spanish documents and issues a body transport permit to the funeral company. Documents should be in Korean or English. Korea is an Apostille Convention party and is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
KR.arrival: The airline's handling agent at Incheon passes the documents to the National Quarantine Station; after quarantine and customs clearance the casket is collected at the cargo terminal, about two hours after landing per the Korean Embassy in Spain, by the receiver with ID and a pre-arranged hearse (terminal fee about KRW 150,000 per that embassy). If the cause of death cannot be confirmed or an infectious disease is suspected, the quarantine station chief may order an autopsy and may restrict the funeral method (Art. 25(4)-(5)). The death must then be reported in Korea within one month. Cremated remains are exempt from customs and quarantine clearance on entry (Korean Embassy in Poland).
KR.private_aviation: The Quarantine Act applies to any aircraft: whoever brings a body into Korea must submit the documents to the quarantine station chief, and a death occurring on board in flight must be reported with a death circumstance report (Enforcement Rule Art. 20). Land at an airport with quarantine and customs (Incheon, Gimpo, Gimhae and other international airports) and have the handling agent arrange quarantine and customs clearance of the casket before departure.
KR.export: Police investigate deaths. For non-natural deaths, the police and a prosecutor must approve release, and the police issue a completion-of-examination certificate (geomsi piljeung), which the hospital needs before releasing the body. The hospital issues the death certificate. A post-mortem by the National Forensic Service is mandatory for foreign nationals unless the cause of death is already established; the report can take up to 3 months, but repatriation does not wait for it. For the UK, documents are a translated, notarised and apostilled death certificate, embalming certificate, non-contagious disease certificate, transfer permit and the original passport.
KR.authority: Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, National Quarantine Stations (Incheon Airport); Korea Customs Service; Korean embassies and consulates

documents: DEH Importation of Human Remains Request Form
Death certificate stating the cause of death and whether it was communicable or non-communicable
Burial transit permit (for a body)
Letter of non-communicable disease (for a body)
Translated copies of any document not in English
Administrative fee: CI$25 / US$31.25 locally, or a US$100 bank draft from overseas, payable to CIG-DEH
KY.coffin: DEH does not publish a casket standard for imported bodies (ashes must travel in a sealed urn or approved container). A hermetically sealed coffin with outer case meets airline rules; burial in Cayman is only in purpose-built vaults in designated cemeteries.
KY.embalming: Not specified by DEH; embalming is normally expected for international transport. Confirm with the receiving funeral home.
KY.consular: The Cayman Islands have no consulates of their own; UK missions handle consular matters. No legalisation is required by DEH, but documents not in English must be translated.
KY.arrival: Present the DEH approval letter to Customs when the remains arrive. For a body brought in for burial, the funeral home issues the burial order; nothing is required from the General Registry. Any disposition needs a burial order. Public cemetery vaults: CI$1,200 adult, CI$600 child (DEH).
KY.private_aviation: Private flights clear customs and immigration at Owen Roberts International Airport (Grand Cayman) or Charles Kirkconnell International Airport (Cayman Brac). The DEH approval letter must be in hand and shown to Customs on arrival; no other private-flight rule was found.
KY.export: Leaving the Cayman Islands, the funeral home obtains the registered death certificate, embalming and any removal documents and meets the destination's requirements. No official page on export permits was found.
KY.authority: Department of Environmental Health (DEH), Cayman Islands Government; Customs and Border Control

documents: Death certificate from the country of death, with translation (confirm with consulate)
Embalming certificate (expected; confirm)
Certificate that the death was not caused by a contagious disease (expected; confirm)
Zinc sealing certificate and list of accompanying items (expected; confirm)
Export permit from the country of death
Passport of the deceased
KZ.coffin: Not published officially for entry. Kazakhstan requires an airtight, sealed zinc coffin for bodies leaving the country, and the same standard should be expected for incoming coffins; confirm with the Kazakh consulate.
KZ.embalming: Mandatory for repatriation from Kazakhstan; expected for incoming bodies. Confirm with the Kazakh consulate.
KZ.consular: Kazakhstan is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Contact the Kazakh embassy or consulate in the country of death about consular certification, legalisation or apostille and Kazakh or Russian translations.
KZ.arrival: Not published officially. Expect customs and sanitary-quarantine clearance at the arrival airport and handover to a local funeral service. Kazakhstan's first crematorium opened in Almaty in April 2026, with strict consent conditions.
KZ.private_aviation: No official rule specific to human remains on private aircraft was found. Plan arrival at an international airport with customs, border and sanitary-quarantine control, and have the handling agent confirm clearance of the coffin in advance.
KZ.export: The death is registered at a registry office; the certificate is in Kazakh and Russian, without the cause of death, and can be apostilled. A post-mortem is usually done within 24 hours (it can be waived in some supervised natural deaths). Repatriation needs embalming, the death certificate, permission to remove the body from the mortuary or forensic facility, an airtight sealed zinc coffin, a funeral director's letter that the coffin contains no foreign objects with a list of accompanying items, a Health Inspection Services certificate confirming embalming, and Customs Department permission.
KZ.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kazakhstan (consular service); Health Inspection Services and Customs for exit

documents: Original death certificate
Burial transit permit
Letter of non-contagious disease from an authorised health institution
Letter of embalming
Letter of sealed casket
Original passport of the deceased and Lebanese ID or civil registry extract
Death registration form signed by a family member
LB.coffin: A letter confirming the casket is sealed is required by the Lebanese embassy; use a hermetically sealed, zinc-lined casket in an outer wooden case meeting airline requirements. Who witnesses the sealing is not specified.
LB.embalming: The Lebanese embassy in Washington requires a letter of embalming; the embassy in the Netherlands lists the embalming certificate as optional. Confirm with the consulate handling the case.
LB.consular: The Lebanese embassy or consulate reviews the documents and issues the mortuary pass (Netherlands embassy, consular fee EUR 44); the Washington embassy exempts transfers of remains and death registration from consular fees from 1 March 2026. The death is also registered with the Lebanese civil registry through the consulate.
LB.arrival: Customs and health clearance at Beirut airport; the receiving funeral director or family collects. Burial takes place in religious burial grounds; cremation is generally prohibited in Lebanon.
LB.private_aviation: No official rule specific to private flights carrying human remains was found. Beirut-Rafic Hariri is the international port of entry; airspace can be disrupted during regional hostilities. Confirm clearance with the handling agent.
LB.export: The hospital issues a death attestation; the local Mukhtar issues the death certificate (signed and stamped by the certifying doctor) and the death is registered at the local registry office. A post-mortem needs General Prosecutor approval and the family's permission. Repatriation requires the death certificate, the deceased's passport, a no-objection letter from the deceased's embassy and Ministry of Health permission. Cremation is not available.
LB.authority: Lebanese embassy/consulate abroad; Ministry of Health (exit)

documents: Official certificate of cause of death from the registrar of deaths or similar authority
Statement by the person who prepared the remains, certified by an appropriate authority, describing the preparation and confirming the coffin holds only the body, clothing and packing
Transit permit from the competent authority at the place of death, stating the deceased's names and age
Documents in the official language (English) of Saint Lucia
Environmental health officer's clearance at the port of entry
LC.coffin: Remains must be placed in a hermetically sealed impervious coffin; an outer wooden box or special fabric may be added for protection. Alternatively an embalmed body may be sealed in a plastic container placed in a non-impervious coffin. A durable plaque on the outside must show the name, age and final destination.
LC.embalming: The law allows either thorough disinfection (orifices packed, body wrapped in a disinfectant sheet) in an impervious coffin, or arterial and cavity embalming. Embalming is mandatory if the deceased had a quarantinable disease.
LC.consular: No consular legalisation step is set out in the regulations; documents must be in English. Ask the Saint Lucia mission in the country of death whether authentication is expected.
LC.arrival: Human remains may not leave the port of entry until an environmental health officer issues clearance (prescribed form). Copies of the documents must travel with the remains or reach the environmental health officer within 24 hours. The local funeral director collects. No legal burial deadline found.
LC.private_aviation: No private-flight rules found. Land at a port of entry where an environmental health officer can issue the clearance; arrange it in advance, especially outside office hours.
LC.export: Leaving Saint Lucia: the death is registered at the Registry of Civil Status; the certificate (English, with cause of death) is usually issued within 2 days of the post-mortem, which is usually within a week. The same regulations apply to anyone transporting remains: documents go to the Chief Medical Officer, a $250 fee is paid to the Accountant General, and the Chief Medical Officer's certificate must appear on the outside of the coffin.
LC.authority: Ministry of Health: Chief Medical Officer and Environmental Health officers

documents: Laissez-passer (Leichenpass) for the corpse from the country of death (Berlin or Strasbourg party states)
Death certificate from the country of death, with translation if needed
From other countries: documents required by the Swiss arrival authorities (to be confirmed with the Swiss or Liechtenstein authorities)
LI.coffin: For Strasbourg or Berlin transfers, a sealed coffin meeting the agreement (zinc-lined inner coffin with absorbent material in a wooden coffin). Liechtenstein's own rules for coffins from other countries were not verified.
LI.embalming: Not verified for Liechtenstein; follow the departure country's rules.
LI.consular: From Berlin or Strasbourg states no consular step is normally needed. From other countries, ask the Swiss or Liechtenstein authorities whether legalised documents are required. The UK covers Liechtenstein from its embassy in Switzerland.
LI.arrival: The coffin clears customs at the Swiss arrival airport; Switzerland and Liechtenstein form one customs area, so there is no further customs border on the road to Liechtenstein. Swiss and Liechtenstein funeral directors handle the transfer. The Swiss Epidemics Act also applies in Liechtenstein.
LI.private_aviation: There is no airport in Liechtenstein. Plan the flight to a Swiss airport with customs (Zurich, or St. Gallen-Altenrhein near the border), meet the funeral director airside and continue by hearse. Swiss rules on human remains apply to the flight.
LI.export: The death is registered at the Liechtenstein civil registry office (Zivilstandsamt, Vaduz), which issues an international death certificate without cause of death. For a transfer to the UK, the family needs the death certificate, permission to remove the body and the passport; the body leaves by road to a Swiss or Austrian airport. The Liechtenstein authority that issues the Leichenpass was not verified (likely the health authorities; confirm). In Switzerland the cantons designate the Leichenpass authority (for example the civil registry office in Zug since 2025).
LI.authority: Liechtenstein Government (Amt fur Gesundheit, not verified) and Zivilstandsamt; Swiss authorities at the arrival airport

documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death (coroner's certificate where applicable)
Health authority certificate that the death was not from a contagious or quarantinable disease (including Covid-19)
Embalming certificate from the funeral director or health authority, stating the body is packed as required and the coffin contains only the deceased
Coffin-closing authorisation and coffin certificate from the undertaker
Police report, coroner's certificate or forensic report for unnatural deaths
Sri Lankan passport of the deceased (cancelled by the mission)
Next of kin's written request and affidavit attested by a Justice of the Peace
No-objection letter from the Sri Lankan embassy or high commission
Prior approval of the Airport Health Officer (APHO), Bandaranaike International Airport
LK.coffin: The body must be embalmed and placed in a hardwood coffin with a lead or zinc lining. If it is not embalmed, it must be packed in a hardwood coffin with a hermetically sealed lead or zinc lining, with disinfectant (chloride of lime or zinc sulphate mixed with sawdust) filling the empty spaces. Missions ask for a coffin-closing authorisation from the undertaker. No official witness is mentioned.
LK.embalming: Sri Lankan missions (for example Geneva and Canberra) ask for an embalming certificate or a certificate that the body is preserved as required. The rules also allow an unembalmed body in a hardwood coffin with a hermetically sealed lead or zinc lining packed with disinfectant. Confirm with the mission handling the case.
LK.consular: The Sri Lankan mission issues a no-objection letter after receiving the next of kin's request and Justice-of-the-Peace affidavit, the documents and the cancelled passport. The letter is free for Sri Lankan citizens; Canberra charges AUD 45 for former citizens. All documents must be in English or come with a certified English translation. Repatriation is limited to Sri Lankan nationals, former citizens, and foreigners married to, or children of, Sri Lankan citizens.
LK.arrival: The airline submits the documents to the APHO at Bandaranaike International Airport, which aims to approve within one working day. No remains may be flown without this approval. Remains are released at the airport to the consignee; an affidavit is needed to release them to another nominated person. Unnatural deaths may need an inquest at District General Hospital Negombo before release. The Director of Quarantine may restrict or refuse remains linked to a communicable disease.
LK.private_aviation: Remains must enter through Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA), and the APHO must approve them before departure. On a private flight, the operator or handling agent must obtain this approval, a role normally filled by the airline (not confirmed for private flights).
LK.export: To take a body out of Sri Lanka, you need: a death certificate (issued after the attending doctor or Judicial Medical Officer completes a Notice of Death and the death is registered with the local Registrar), an embalming certificate, and an export permit for human remains. Local authorities must authorise release, and suspicious deaths may be referred to the Magistrates' Court. Once all documents are available, repatriation generally takes 3 to 4 working days. Local funeral directors usually handle the formalities.
LK.authority: Airport Health Officer, Bandaranaike International Airport (Ministry of Health); Sri Lankan missions (Consular Affairs Division, Ministry of Foreign Affairs)

documents: Letter from the funeral home describing the transport arrangements
Copy of the funeral home licence
Embalming affidavit
Burial transit permit
Certified copy of the death certificate
Non-contagious disease letter
Non-contraband letter
Passport of the deceased
Flight itinerary
Liberian Mortuary Certificate application form (with photo of the deceased and receiving funeral home in Liberia)
LR.coffin: No Liberian specification published. The non-contraband letter implies the casket must contain only the remains. Airlines usually expect a hermetically sealed casket in an outer case; confirm with the embassy.
LR.embalming: Required for the Mortuary Certificate: an embalming affidavit is on the embassy checklist.
LR.consular: The Liberian embassy issues a Mortuary Certificate ('notarial certificate to transport human remains'). Washington fee: US$150, plus US$50 for next-day rush, in US currency. The form asks for the remitting and the receiving funeral homes, airline, flight number and arrival date. Not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
LR.arrival: Clearance at Roberts International Airport (Monrovia); the receiving Liberian funeral home named on the Mortuary Certificate collects. Local burial or cremation formalities for an incoming casket were not verified: confirm with the receiving funeral home and the embassy.
LR.private_aviation: No rules specific to private flights carrying remains were found. Land at Roberts International Airport with customs and carry the Mortuary Certificate and original documents with the casket; the form asks for flight details, so give the private flight details.
LR.export: UK guidance: funeral directors repatriate only with authorisation from the embassy, the next of kin or authorised person, and a consulate mortuary certificate. Remains of a person who died in Liberia may only be buried, cremated or otherwise disposed of with a permit to handle the body from the registrar of the district of death (Public Health Law: within 24 hours of the certificate). Death certificates are issued only by the Bureau of Vital and Health Statistics, Ministry of Health, within 7 working days of an interview; unknown causes need a court affidavit, road deaths a police report. When the body is repatriated, it is preserved by embalming rather than cold storage.
LR.authority: Embassy of Liberia (Mortuary Certificate); Ministry of Health, Bureau of Vital and Health Statistics (local deaths)

documents: Laissez-passer for the transfer of a corpse from the country of death (Strasbourg Agreement states)
Death certificate / official information on the death abroad for the civil registrar
Transport permit from the departure authority (needed by the registrar to authorise burial)
From non-Strasbourg countries: documents to be confirmed with the Luxembourg embassy or consulate
LU.coffin: Between Strasbourg Agreement states the coffin must meet the Agreement's requirements (leak-proof coffin with absorbent material, typically a zinc inner coffin in a wooden outer coffin). For overland transport between the Netherlands and Luxembourg, the Dutch rules require only a watertight coffin. Luxembourg's own coffin rules for other origins were not verified.
LU.embalming: No Luxembourg embalming requirement for incoming bodies was verified; follow the departure country's rules.
LU.consular: From Strasbourg states no consular step is normally required. Luxembourg missions (or Belgian missions where Luxembourg is not represented) can help families obtain or legalise local documents; repatriation costs are paid by the family, an insurer or a mutual association.
LU.arrival: For a death abroad, the civil registrar of the commune of registration authorises burial in writing on the basis of the official information on the death that it judges sufficient. Burial normally between the 24th and 72nd hour after death; an extension can be granted on a medical inspector's certificate. Cremation rules for a body arriving from abroad were not verified: confirm with the commune.
LU.private_aviation: Arrive at Luxembourg Airport (Findel) with customs, the receiving funeral director meeting the aircraft. Human remains on a private flight need the same papers as airline cargo. The coffin must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
LU.export: To send a body abroad to a Strasbourg party state, the laissez-passer is issued by the competent authority Luxembourg designated under the Agreement: Direction de la Santé, Division de l'Inspection sanitaire.
