TZ.arrival: Arrival procedure is not published. Keep the original authenticated documents and the embassy permit with the coffin for clearance at the arrival airport; a family member or Tanzanian funeral home collects. No national burial deadline was found.
TZ.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. Human remains need the same documents as on an airline (originals with the coffin), and the aircraft should land at an international airport with customs and health services; usual landing and overflight permissions for foreign-registered aircraft apply. Zanzibar has its own authorities; confirm with the receiving funeral home whether additional clearance is needed.
TZ.export: Per the UK FCDO bereavement guide, local undertakers provide the special casket for international carriage, and shipping requires a civil registry death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains abroad. TZ.authority: Tanzanian embassy or high commission abroad (entry); civil registry and local authorities in Tanzania (exit)

UA.coffin: No official entry rule found; confirm with the Ukrainian consulate. For remains leaving Ukraine, a hermetically sealed zinc casket is required and must be sealed by a Ukrainian customs official.
UA.embalming: No official entry rule found; the country of death or airline may require it. Inside Ukraine, local morticians prefer to embalm within 48 hours, and burial may be delayed for a reasonable period if the body is embalmed.
UA.consular: No official Ukrainian consular procedure for incoming remains could be opened. Contact the Ukrainian embassy or consulate in the country of death about certification and translations.
UA.arrival: Arrival by road from Poland (or another neighbour) through a border crossing with customs. A Ukrainian funeral home collects the casket. Burial is normally permitted only in the place of residence; burial elsewhere needs prior permission from the central mortuary office in Kyiv and the local authority.
UA.private_aviation: According to the US Embassy, airports in Ukraine are currently not operating, so no flight can land there. Fly to an airport in a neighbouring country (remains are usually handled via Warsaw, Poland) and continue by hearse.
UA.export: Leaving Ukraine: the death must be registered at the local registry office within 3 days; the certificate is issued on the mortuary's medical cause-of-death report and the passport. Remains must be in a hermetically sealed zinc casket; the casket or urn must be sealed by a Ukrainian customs official certifying no illegal items, without which shipping is impossible. Remains are usually driven to Poland (about USD 500 during wartime) and flown from Warsaw. UG.coffin: The Ugandan missions do not set a casket standard: the transporting airline advises on the appropriate casket.
UG.embalming: Embalming is required: a certificate of embalmment is part of the file.
UG.consular: Originals are sent by express mail to the Ugandan mission with a prepaid return envelope; the mission certifies them free of charge (1 to 3 working days in Copenhagen and Mombasa, 1 working day in Washington) and returns them with a cover note. UG.arrival: The certified originals travel with the coffin for clearance at the arrival airport (normally Entebbe International Airport); the family or a Ugandan funeral home collects. No national burial deadline was found.
UG.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. Human remains need the same mission-certified documents as on an airline (originals with the coffin), and the aircraft should land at an international airport with customs and health services, normally Entebbe; usual landing and overflight permissions for foreign-registered aircraft apply. UG.export: Per the UK FCDO, shipping a body from Uganda requires a local civil registry death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains. documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death (required unless embalmed or cremated), with an English translation whose authenticity is attested by a notary or similar official if not in English

Embalming certificate where the body was embalmed (embalmed remains are exempt from the death-certificate and permit requirements)
Export clearance documents required by the country of death
CDC import permit only if the person died of an infectious disease and the remains are not embalmed or cremated
US.coffin: CDC requires all non-cremated remains to be fully contained in a leak-proof container: a double-layered puncture-resistant body bag (two sealed bags, one inside the other), a casket whose interior lining is certified leak-proof and puncture-resistant by the manufacturer, or a sealed metal body transfer case. No witnessed sealing is required by US law; the country of departure or the carrier may impose a hermetically sealed or zinc-lined coffin and an outer air tray.
US.embalming: Not required by US federal rules. Embalming before import removes the need for a death certificate and for any CDC permit, including when the death was caused by an infectious disease. The country of departure often requires embalming anyway.
US.consular: No legalisation or consular visa is required by the US for entry. For a US citizen, the US embassy or consulate abroad can help obtain the documents and may issue a Consular Report of Death Abroad and, where needed, a Consular Mortuary Certificate. The State Department does not pay for repatriation.
US.arrival: CBP clears the remains at the first US port of entry, checking the CDC documents. A licensed US funeral director collects the remains and obtains the local burial-transit or cremation permit under state law. There is no federal burial deadline; timing follows state rules.
US.pouch: Accepted by CDC as a leak-proof container only as a double-layered, puncture-resistant body bag (two sealed bags, one inside the other). The country of departure, the carrier and the receiving funeral home may still require a casket or transfer case.
US.private_aviation: A private aircraft arriving from abroad must transmit the arrival manifest through eAPIS (or another CBP-approved system) no later than 60 minutes before departure and must receive CBP landing approval before leaving the foreign airport; the manifest alone does not grant landing rights. Flights from the south must generally land at the nearest designated airport to the border or coastline crossing. The remains are declared and cleared by CBP on arrival with the same CDC documents.
US.export: Leaving the US: the funeral director obtains the local death certificate and a certificate of embalming (or cremation), plus the documents required by the destination country (for example a disposition permit, non-contagious disease letter, apostille or consular legalisation; confirm with the destination's consulate). Release can be delayed when a medical examiner investigates a sudden, unexpected or unattended death, or when there is a criminal investigation.
US.authority: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); US Customs and Border Protection (CBP); state vital records offices

documents: MSP entry request form, filed by the Uruguayan funeral home at least 12 h before arrival
Death certificate (acta de defuncion), apostilled
Certificate of embalming and hermetic sealing of the coffin, apostilled
Sanitary transport authorisation from the country of death
Certificate stating whether death was due to an infectious or contagious disease
Letter from a relative requesting the transfer, copy of the deceased's ID or passport, flight itinerary
Spanish translation of documents in other languages
UY.coffin: Hermetically sealed coffin; the Uruguayan consulate asks for an apostilled certificate of embalming and hermetic sealing issued by the funeral provider. No rule on who witnesses the sealing was found.
UY.embalming: Expected: consulates ask for an embalming certificate, and MSP Ordinance 982/2016 requires a conservation and preparation record when remains travel on collective (public) transport.
UY.consular: Contact the Uruguayan consulate in the country of death before arranging transport; it reviews the documents (free consular procedure). Documents must be apostilled and translated into Spanish.
UY.arrival: MSP issues an entry authorisation certificate to the funeral home electronically. If death was due to an infectious disease, the body cannot be shipped until the authorisation is issued. Frozen bodies or bodies leaking fluids are not admitted unless bagged. Ashes need no sanitary authorisation.
UY.private_aviation: The MSP request is filed with the Sanidad Aerea unit at Carrasco airport (sanidadaerea@msp.gub.uy) for air arrivals. Ordinance 982/2016 ties the conservation record to collective transport, but consulates still ask for embalming. Confirm health clearance if landing at another airport (e.g. Punta del Este).
UY.export: The local funeral director handles exit. Documents: doctor's or forensic death certificate, civil registry death certificate (usually a couple of days), conservation certificate from the Sanitation Department (Direccion de Salubridad) of the Intendencia, next-of-kin authorisation, air waybill, and legalisation by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs with translation. Formalities may take some days.
UY.authority: Ministerio de Salud Publica (Departamento de Vigilancia en Fronteras / Sanidad Aerea); Uruguayan consulates abroad

documents: Death certificate from the country of death, with translation (confirm with consulate)
Embalming certificate (expected; confirm)
Certificate that the death was not caused by a contagious disease (expected; confirm)
Zinc sealing certificate (expected; confirm)
Export permit from the country of death
Passport of the deceased
UZ.coffin: Not published officially for entry. Uzbekistan requires an airproof sealed zinc coffin (container) for bodies leaving the country; expect the same on entry and confirm with the Uzbek consulate.
UZ.embalming: Mandatory for repatriation from Uzbekistan; expected for incoming bodies. Embalming and refrigeration facilities in Uzbekistan are limited, so the body should arrive properly embalmed.
UZ.consular: Uzbekistan is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Contact the Uzbek embassy or consulate in the country of death about consular certification, legalisation or apostille and Uzbek or Russian translations.
UZ.arrival: Not published officially. Expect customs and sanitary clearance at the arrival airport (normally Tashkent) and handover to a local funeral service. Burial usually takes place within 48 hours of death. There are no cremation facilities in Uzbekistan.
UZ.private_aviation: No official rule specific to human remains on private aircraft was found. Plan arrival at an international airport with customs, border and sanitary-quarantine control, and have the handling agent confirm clearance of the coffin in advance.
UZ.export: A post-mortem is usually done within 24 hours and the mortuary or forensic institute issues a medical certificate of death, which is often enough for repatriation; ZAGS issues the death certificate in Uzbek and Russian in 1 to 3 days. Repatriation needs embalming, an airproof sealed zinc coffin delivered to the airport cargo terminal at least 4 hours before the flight, customs permission, a funeral director's act that no foreign objects were in the coffin with a list of accompanying items, and a Health Inspection Services certificate. A no-objection letter from the deceased's embassy is sometimes required.
UZ.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Uzbekistan (consular service); Customs and Health Inspection Services for exit

documents: Official certificate of the cause of death (original)
Certificate that the deceased did not have a contagious disease at death (original)
Embalming certificate (original)
Passport or official ID of the deceased
VC.coffin: Hermetically sealed impervious coffin required for burial. No official witnessing of the sealing is described.
VC.embalming: Required: an embalming certificate must be presented to the officials in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
VC.consular: The SVG High Commission guidance asks for originals of all documents; no legalisation step is described. Many routings transit Barbados, so that country's transit requirements must also be checked.
VC.arrival: The official in SVG responsible for entry of human remains must be given the arrival time and flight number and advises on charges. The local funeral home collects after clearance. No legal burial deadline found.
VC.private_aviation: No rules specific to private flights found. A direct private flight avoids the usual transhipment via Barbados; still give the SVG entry official the flight details and arrival time in advance and land at an airport of entry.
VC.export: Leaving SVG: the death is registered at the Civil Registry (Kingstown or the district); copies take about 2 days. A magistrate issues the medical warrant and, after a post-mortem, the warrant to bury. The local funeral director provides the embalming certificate, transit documents and permission to transfer the remains.
VC.authority: Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines official for entry of human remains (health authorities)

documents: Application for Burial / importation and exportation of body form (Ministry of Health and Social Development)
Authentic death certificate stating the cause of death (or cremation certificate for ashes)
Burial permit from the BVI Civil Registry
Embalming certificate and removal permit of the country of death (expected by airlines; not listed by the Ministry)
Ministry letter of approval and Importation Certificate (issued within two working days)
VG.coffin: Not specified by the Ministry. A hermetically sealed coffin with outer case meets airline rules; confirm with the receiving funeral home.
VG.embalming: Not specified by the Ministry; embalming is expected for international transport.
VG.consular: The BVI have no consulates of their own; UK missions handle consular matters. No legalisation requirement is published; the death certificate must be authentic and state the cause of death.
VG.arrival: Present the Ministry's letter of approval and Importation Certificate on arrival; the receiving funeral home arranges customs clearance and burial under the Civil Registry burial permit.
VG.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at Terrance B. Lettsome International Airport (Beef Island) with customs clearance arranged and the Importation Certificate in hand; have the funeral home meet the aircraft. No specific rule for private flights carrying remains was found.
VG.export: Leaving the BVI: submit the same burial application form in person or by email to the Ministry of Health and Social Development with the death certificate (stating the cause of death) and/or cremation certificate; an exportation schedule and permission letter are issued, to be collected within two days. No fee.
VG.authority: Ministry of Health and Social Development, Government of the Virgin Islands; Civil Registry

documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death (English or with a translation), unless the remains are embalmed
Embalming certificate where the body is embalmed
Consular Report of Death Abroad or Consular Mortuary Certificate from the US embassy if the deceased was a US citizen
Removal or export permit from the country of departure
Passport of the deceased and air waybill or flight manifest
Name and contact of the receiving licensed funeral home in US Virgin Islands
VI.coffin: CDC requires all non-cremated remains to be fully contained in a leak-proof container (for example a casket with a leak-proof lining or a sealed metal transfer case). No territorial rule on zinc lining or witnessed sealing was found; the country of departure may impose a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin.
VI.embalming: Not required by US federal rules for entry, but embalmed remains are exempt from the CDC death-certificate requirement. Remains of a person who died of certain infectious diseases may need a CDC import permit unless embalmed. Most departure countries and airlines require embalming anyway.
VI.consular: No legalisation is required for entry. If a US citizen dies abroad, the US embassy or consulate can issue a Consular Report of Death Abroad and, where no death certificate exists, a Consular Mortuary Certificate. Foreign-language documents need an English translation.
VI.arrival: CBP clears the remains at the first US port of entry, with CDC requirements checked against the documents. Under 42 CFR 71.55 the remains must go directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory. The receiving funeral home then handles the local burial or cremation formalities with the Virgin Islands Department of Health Office of Vital Records and Statistics; the territory's own requirements are not published online.
VI.private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. An international arrival into US Virgin Islands must clear US Customs and Border Protection, so plan the flight to an airport where CBP clearance can be arranged in advance and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. A flight from the US mainland is a domestic flight and needs no CBP entry, but the state burial-transit permit must travel with the remains.
VI.export: Not published online. The Department of Health Office of Vital Records and Statistics registers deaths and works with funeral homes; a licensed funeral home normally obtains the death certificate and a removal or burial-transit permit before departure. For destinations outside the US, the destination consulate's requirements (embalming, sealed coffin, legalisation) apply. Confirm with the Office of Vital Records (St Thomas or St Croix).
VI.authority: US CDC and CBP (entry); Virgin Islands Department of Health, Office of Vital Records and Statistics (exit)

documents: Vietnamese embassy permit application form (with landing airport, carrier, flight number and arrival time)
Written consent of the local People's Committee in Vietnam where the body will be buried, obtained by a relative in Vietnam
Death certificate (certified copy)
Applicant's passport or ID and proof of relationship
Deceased's passport and proof of Vietnamese origin where relevant
Certificate of no infectious or contagious disease and local quarantine / transit permit
Funeral director certificate that only the body is in the casket
VN.coffin: Vietnamese law (Ministry of Health Circular 21/2021) requires a three-layer coffin for cross-border transport: an inner layer of zinc or other non-leaking load-bearing material, lined with absorbent and hermetically sealed; a wooden middle layer; and a plywood outer layer. Vietnamese embassy guidance (Ottawa, New Delhi) describes a zinc-covered coffin lined with PVC sheets and absorbent material, placed in an outer wooden case sealed by security and health authorities in the country of departure.
VN.embalming: Not explicitly required by the embassy pages consulted. Vietnamese hygiene rules limit holding a body to 48 hours without refrigeration and 7 days refrigerated at 4 C or below, so embalming is in practice expected for air transport.
VN.consular: The Vietnamese embassy or consulate in the country of death issues the entry permit (Circular 01/2011: within 1 working day of a complete file; embassies in Ottawa and New Delhi announce 5 to 7 business days). The permit also cancels the deceased's Vietnamese passport and is notified to border customs and immigration. Group A infectious disease deaths (e.g. Ebola, cholera, SARS, plague) are refused.
VN.arrival: Border customs and health quarantine at the arrival airport check the permit and documents before release to the family or funeral service. Remains must comply with Vietnamese customs and quarantine law.
VN.private_aviation: The embassy permit application names the arrival airport, carrier, flight number and arrival time, so a private flight must be scheduled before the permit is requested. Use an international airport with customs and health quarantine.
VN.export: To take a body out of Vietnam, the funeral director obtains an international medical quarantine certificate (in Hanoi from the International Centre for Disease Control) and permission from the Quarantine and Customs and Immigration Office; a certificate of preservation, the death certificate and passport are also needed. Local authorities require a diplomatic note from the deceased's embassy confirming the family's wishes. Hospitals normally embalm. Local formalities take about one week (gov.uk); the death certificate takes about a week.
VN.authority: Vietnamese embassy or consulate (Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Consular Department); local People's Committee; border health quarantine

documents: Official letter of request from the family to the CEO of MPMC
Medical cause of death
Embalming certificate from the mortuary or funeral parlour
Death registry certificate
Coroner's report (mainly where the cause of death is an infectious disease)
Identification of the deceased (passport photo page, ID or birth certificate)
Declaration of any natural flowers, tapa, fine mats or treated-wood casket (for Quarantine)
WS.coffin: No casket specification for whole bodies is published in the policy; a sealed casket meeting airline rules is expected. Treated-wood caskets must be declared for Quarantine. Disinterred bones must be chemically sterilised and hermetically sealed.
WS.embalming: Required: an embalming certificate is part of the required documents.
WS.consular: Applications can be lodged through Samoa's overseas missions or directly with MPMC; the administrative fee can be paid to MPMC or to the mission in local currency. The approval letter is collected by family in Samoa or sent to the mission.
WS.arrival: Border agency officers at the regulated port of entry (Faleolo) clear the remains after normal arrivals. The airline submits the air waybill for Customs and Quarantine clearance and the accompanying family presents the approval letter. Where a coroner's report is needed, the Ministry of Health may set the burial date.
WS.private_aviation: The policy applies at all regulated ports of entry. For a private flight, obtain the MPMC approval letter before departure, arrive at Faleolo with border agencies present, and carry the approval letter and documents for Customs and Quarantine.
WS.export: No official procedure for sending a body out of Samoa was found. Expect the death registry certificate, medical cause of death and embalming, plus the destination country's consular requirements; confirm with the Ministry of Health.
WS.authority: Ministry of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, with the Ministry of Health

documents: Local death certificate (transcription into French civil status by the consulate recommended)
Medical certificate of cause of death or non-contagion certificate
Embalming or conservation certificate where required by the departure country
Transport authorisation from the French embassy or consulate (from abroad) or from the prefect where the coffin is closed (from mainland France or another DOM)
Coffin closure/sealing certificate
Details of the receiving funeral director and cemetery or crematorium
YT.coffin: Airtight coffin with a metal box (in practice soldered zinc inside a wooden coffin) is mandatory for air transport under French rules. A hermetic coffin complicates later cremation.
YT.embalming: French rules do not impose embalming for an incoming body; the departure country and airline usually require it for long journeys.
YT.consular: From abroad, entry into France (including overseas departments) and transport to the place of burial or cremation require authorisation from the French embassy or consulate. France is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement; whether a Strasbourg laissez-passer alone suffices for this department is not stated, confirm with the consulate. Families bear all costs.
YT.arrival: The receiving funeral director takes the coffin at the airport. French law (CGCT art. R2213-33) sets burial or cremation no later than the 14th calendar day after the body enters the territory of the overseas department when it comes from abroad; the prefect may grant exceptions. Most of the population is Muslim and families usually seek a rapid burial; prepare paperwork before the flight.
YT.private_aviation: Same documents as airline cargo; the coffin must be airtight for any air transport. Plan arrival at Dzaoudzi-Pamandzi international airport, with customs (douane) and border police, and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft. The runway at Dzaoudzi-Pamandzi is short, which limits some long-range jets; check aircraft performance with the operator.
YT.export: The funeral company handles formalities. To mainland France or abroad, the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed authorises the transport; air transport requires an airtight coffin. Ashes need authorisation from the prefect of the place of cremation or of the applicant's residence. The destination country's consular rules also apply.
YT.authority: French embassy or consulate abroad (entry from abroad); Prefect of Mayotte (exit) and prefect where the coffin is closed

documents: Import permit from the National Department of Health, applied for by email to humanremainspermits@health.gov.za (valid 30 days)
Cover letter from the embassy or funeral undertaker naming the deceased, place of burial, date, place and cause of death, the South African point of entry and the type of transport
Death certificate clearly stating the cause of death (certified English translation if needed)
ID document or passport of the deceased
Embalming certificate (or statement of the alternative preservation method if embalming is refused for religious reasons)
Letter from a family member requesting the import, with their ID or passport and contact details
Non-infectious (or infectious) disease certificate signed by a registered medical practitioner or forensic pathologist
Certificate of Competence of the South African funeral undertaker who will receive the remains
ZA.coffin: For non-infectious remains, the body is sealed in an airtight container and placed in a sturdy, non-transparent coffin. Infectious remains must also be placed in a polythene bag, and their sealed container may not be opened without approval of the medical officer (Regulation R363, reg. 12).
ZA.embalming: Embalming is required and certified. If embalming cannot be done for religious reasons, a statement from the relevant authority describing the alternative preservation method must be supplied. Bodies of persons who died of smallpox, anthrax or viral haemorrhagic fever must not be embalmed.
ZA.consular: A South African embassy or the funeral undertaker can submit the permit application; the Consulate General in New York, for example, sends a request letter with the deceased's particulars to Pretoria. Documents not in English need a certified translation. South Africa is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
ZA.arrival: Port Health (Border Management Authority) detains and inspects human remains on arrival and grants clearance only once permit conditions are met. Remains arriving without a permit can be held in a mortuary at the importer's cost and, if no permit follows within 30 days, buried by order of the Director-General. A certified local undertaker receives the coffin.
ZA.private_aviation: The permit application must name the point of entry and the type of transport, so a private flight must land at the declared port of entry with Port Health (Border Management Authority) presence. The regulations require an airtight container in a sealed coffin on public transport and an approved coffin or container otherwise; confirm acceptable containers with the Department of Health.
ZA.export: Leaving South Africa also requires an export permit from the National Department of Health (applied for by email; about 2 working days once complete). The file includes a cover letter naming the exit point and transport, death certificate with cause of death, ID or passport (or a police affidavit), an embalming certificate stamped by the undertaker and embalmer with the address of the embalming premises, a family request letter, a non-infectious disease certificate, the Notice of Death form (BI-1663), the Burial Order from the Department of Home Affairs and the undertaker's Certificate of Competence.
ZA.authority: National Department of Health (Director-General of Health); Port Health, Border Management Authority

documents: Application with the deceased's name and details, reason for the request and tentative transport schedule
Names and addresses of the Zambian residents responsible for the remains in Zambia
Notarised statement from the local health authority that there is no danger of infection
Notarised statement from the local health authority that the body is in a hermetically sealed casket and wooden outer box
Locally issued burial and/or transit permit
Certified copy of the death certificate
ZM.coffin: Hermetically sealed casket inside a wooden outer box, attested by a notarised statement from the local health authority of the country of death.
ZM.embalming: The Zambian embassy checklist (Washington) does not list embalming. Airlines and departure countries usually require it; confirm with the Zambian embassy.
ZM.consular: Contact the Zambian embassy's consular section and send a scanned application package; prior written consent comes from the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Lusaka. No fee or processing time is published. Zambia is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
ZM.arrival: The application must name the Zambian residents who will take charge of the remains. Arrival clearance details are not published; originals should travel with the coffin for customs and health checks.
ZM.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. Human remains travel with the same documents as on an airline (originals with the coffin), and the aircraft should land at an international airport with customs, immigration and port-health officers on duty; usual landing and overflight permissions for foreign-registered aircraft apply. The zinc-lined coffin (about 2.2 m, often 100 kg or more) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin). Main international airports include Lusaka (Kenneth Kaunda) and Ndola.
ZM.export: The UK FCDO guide covers death registration (Registrar General, Lusaka, or local Boma offices; certificates in English, collectable within 48 hours), body identification and release from the morgue by the next of kin or a nominee. It does not detail export permits, embalming or coffin rules or timelines; the funeral director handles them. Post-mortems and police cases can delay release.
ZM.authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Lusaka (Permanent Secretary), via Zambian embassies

documents: Original death certificate
Original post-mortem report
Original embalming certificate
Original non-infectious diseases certificate
Original permit to repatriate (removal permit) from the country of death
Zimbabwean passport of the deceased (or national ID/birth certificate plus next-of-kin nationality affidavit)
Funeral home affidavit that the consignment is non-hazardous and non-flammable
Affidavit or letter from a family representative requesting burial in Zimbabwe
ZW.coffin: The Zimbabwean embassy pages do not specify casket construction. Follow airline and departure-country rules (normally a hermetically sealed metal-lined coffin in a wooden case).
ZW.embalming: Embalming is required: an embalming certificate is on every embassy checklist.
ZW.consular: Send originals and copies to the Zimbabwean embassy (Washington: US$35 fee, about 5 business days, forwarded to head office for a health certificate; Ankara: US$10). If the deceased had no Zimbabwean passport, the embassy seeks clearance from Harare first. Zimbabwe is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
ZW.arrival: The embassy-stamped original documents must accompany the remains for clearance on arrival. Who collects is the family or a Zimbabwean funeral parlour; arrival procedures are not published.
ZW.private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. Human remains travel with the same documents as on an airline (originals with the coffin), and the aircraft should land at an international airport with customs, immigration and port-health officers on duty; usual landing and overflight permissions for foreign-registered aircraft apply. The zinc-lined coffin (about 2.2 m, often 100 kg or more) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin). Main ports of entry include Harare (Robert Gabriel Mugabe International), Bulawayo and Victoria Falls.
ZW.export: Per the UK FCDO, the death is registered with the Registrar General's Office (certificate within about one working week; BD12 medical certificate or BD11 police notice of death as applicable). Shipping requires the civil registry death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains. Rural mortuary facilities are limited.
ZW.authority: Zimbabwean embassy abroad with head office (Ministry of Foreign Affairs) health certificate; Registrar General (exit)
